articles.title: Young Voters and the 2026 Blue Wave
articles.author: Randy Shaw
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Power of Ongoing Outreach A big story behind the blue election tsunami was the sharp rise in youth voting. According to a leading source , youth turnout was 27% across the nation. It was 30% in battleground states. It was the best midterm youth turnout since 2018. Voters under 30 favored Democrats by a whopping 35%. In contrast, voters over 45 were almost equally divided. That’s why many believe “ the youth vote was key to Democratic Wins in the Midterms .” This sharp turnout increase among an historically under-performing demographic has been building for years. While youth turnout was driven by factors shared by the overall electorate, it also reflected a sophisticated organizing strategy led by over 50 youth-oriented groups. These groups reached out to young voters’ months before the election. This investment in year-round youth outreach and organizing paid dividends on election turnout. Blue Future played a key coordination and training role in building the capacity of 53 youth-oriented activist groups . Nick Guthman and Morgan Stahr co-founded Blue Future in 2018. The group has worked tirelessly to build a foundation for year-round youth organizing designed to increase youth voting turnout. Related: Jane Kim and Nithya Raman Defy the Democratic Establishment—and Win 8 Years of Work Pays Off Here’s how Blue Future described in October what its financial support for the over fifty youth activist groups is designed to accomplish: “ Young people are bringing their skills, networks, cultural fluency, and leadership to the 2026 midterms. They are building infrastructure, training the next cohort of organizers, and deploying their lived expertise in communities traditional campaigns have overlooked. The field shares a consistent and multi-faceted tactical approach while drawing on the distinct assets each constituency brings — Hmong networks in Wisconsin, working-class leadership in rural North Carolina, college-town relational networks, multigenerational Jewish communities in Florida, climate expertise, and the trusted voices students already rely on for guidance .” The group is bringing the type of sophisticated analysis that groups like the New Georgia Project have used to trigger sustained turnout gains In addition to funneling funds to youth activist groups, Blue Future has an Organize for Democracy program that trains students in organizing, phone banking and leadership development. Students selected for the program across the nation spend five hours a week working on campaigns. Check out the Organizing Testimonials on the group’s website. These students made 1.2 million calls to voters in 2026! Why Year-Round Outreach on Local Issues Matter Blue Future’s strategy confirms what I argue in a recent story I wrote for Social Policy : investing in ongoing organizing is the best strategy for winning elections (See “ Can We Reverse the Decline in Community Organizing? ”). Here’s how Ohio Student Action describes the connection: “ Across the state, our chapters work hard to make the change they want to see in their communities a reality – whether that’s campus reform, local ballot initiatives, or the state budget, OSA is there. Our mission is simple: create an Ohio where students and young people thrive, and fight for a government that saves a seat for us at the table. ” Young people who get involved in community-based political fights are more likely to see the value in voting. And encourage their family and friends to do so. Related: Prop 40 and the Price of Progressive Disunity More Work to Do The estimated national voter turnout was 53%. So a youth turnout of 30% in battleground states shows the need for muchgreater investment in this group. In 1971, the constitutional amendment reducing the eligible voting age from 21 to 18 was signed into law by Richard Nixon. Three-fourths of the states ratified the constitutional amendment in record time. Why the urgency to expand rather than reduce voting rights? The anti-war movement highlighted that people under 21 drafted for the Vietnam War lacked the right to vote. Rather than end the war, the United States lowered the voting age. Instead of relying on foundations or philanthropists, Blue Future has spent years building a small donor list. This is critical for rebuilding the nation’s community organizing infrastructure as well as youth voter turnout. Why did recent U.S. Senate campaigns deluge us with online requests for as little as $3? Small donors add up—if you have a good list. To that end, Blue Future has a nonprofit organization that can receive tax deductible donations for its training and education work. Y ou can donate here . Those under 35 are so directly impacted by government policies that there’s no reason voter turnout should not be higher. Let’s help make that happen for 2028. Beyond Chron

articles.title: Stewards Corner: Laying the Foundation for Change in Your Union
articles.author: Labor Notes Staff
articles.content: Revitalizing a local union may require electing new officers with a different vision. But running for office should not be your first step. Successful campaigns for union office usually start by organizing against management first, often years in advance of any eventual run. A group of workers wants to accomplish something—better pay, more control over their conditions on the job, an end to tiered wages or benefits—but their officials, or something about the way their union operates, is in the way. So they begin to change the culture of the union, getting more members involved in building power on the shop floor. Your ultimate goal, after all, is not just electing new leaders, but building a stronger union. And doing that means involving as many members as possible. WHERE TO START The good news is you can begin organizing for change in your union any time. “Your campaign should start with workplace fights that involve your co-workers,” says John Pearson, a nurse at Highland Hospital in Oakland, California, and former president of the SEIU Local 1021 chapter there. “You need that type of credibility and trust from people to be able to lead successfully.” Before running for office, Pearson helped lead a campaign to defend breaks, involving nurses throughout the Alameda County hospital system, which resulted in a big back pay settlement. He also led an effort to save a substance abuse clinic from defunding. “The word spreads if you’re effective at fighting in the workplace—people know to ask you for help,” says Pearson. This type of organizing shows members that you have a track record, and that collectively members can make a difference. The Caucus of Rank-and-File Educators (CORE), which won leadership in the Chicago Teachers Union in 2010, built up strength in campaigns like a fight to stop the school district from closing dozens of neighborhood schools and replacing them with privately run charters. “So much of our caucus was really forged in the fight against school closings,” says Norine Gutekanst, who was a third-grade teacher at the time. Caucus members attended school closing hearings and teamed up with community activists to camp out all night in front of threatened schools. The leadership of the union, meanwhile, was absent from the fight. CORE was already “doing what the union should have been doing,” said Chicago social studies teacher Bill Lamme. “So when the election came, [CORE activists] didn’t say ‘Elect me and I’ll do this.’ They said, ‘This is what we’ve been doing and we’ll keep doing it.’” ATTEND MEETINGS If you’re serious about getting involved in and transforming your union, you should be regularly attending union meetings, even if the meetings don’t allow for much debate. Bring other members who share your views. By participating, your group can shake things up. “The first time you attend a meeting, just listen,” says Ken Paff, longtime national organizer with Teamsters for a Democratic Union. “Later on,” Paff says, “you can make a proposal, and organize your group to present it. Talk to members before the meeting; draw them in. Get things out to the members, not only to make your group transparent, but also to make union meetings that way. “Tell people there will be a motion on the pension plan, or another burning topic. Ask them to come support the motion. Put it out in writing. Get them to sign a petition in support of it.” In Letter Carriers (NALC) Branch 9 in Minneapolis, a group of members started meeting to talk about how to change the culture of their branch, including its meeting agendas. “We had a president of over 30 years who would just use Robert’s Rules to keep people down,” says letter carrier Chris Pennock. But the group of reformers kept bringing more members to meetings. Eventually their motions started winning. Pennock got 10 minutes on the agenda to talk about fighting post office closures. It was a small step, but a co-worker told him: “I don’t know if you know how historic that is—I’ve never seen a motion pass that the executive board not only didn’t support but were actively opposed to.” Their organizing helped lay the basis to run a reform slate; Pennock is now vice president of Branch 9. “Have faith that you can change the culture,” he says. At the same time, “it’s a mistake to think that meetings are the important thing,” says SEIU Local 1021’s Pearson—especially since most members won’t attend meetings. You want to find other ways to get them involved in the union. “Talk to people in the workplace, especially while you’re working, if you can,” advises Pearson. Some other activities to consider: Holding classes or discussions on issues the union is not addressing Getting members to join rallies or picket lines in solidarity with other unions Organizing a “Vote No” campaign on a subpar contract Campaigning to change your bylaws to make the union more democratic BE AN INFORMATION SOURCE Is your local union run like a small club or clique, with a few insiders making all of the decisions and everyone else wondering what’s going on? Do members feel they don’t have a voice in critical decisions about their jobs, benefits, and contracts? Members want information, and informed members are more active members. You can start building a campaign for change by becoming an information source. Here are some ideas: Inform members about the contract and how to enforce it Take on workplace issues and organize contract enforcement campaigns Organize short gatherings at lunch or after work to talk about workplace or union issues Distribute bulletins on workplace and union issues Hold online or in-person workshops or an educational conference Use an app like WhatsApp to build communication and spread information among members Start a Facebook group to share news about your employer and give members a space to communicate with each other Start an email and text list to send other members news about your local Don’t spread rumors or conspiracy theories. Be reliable and provide information that the members can use. Set a positive and constructive tone, especially if you’re using social media. Remember, your credibility is your most important asset. GETTING MEMBERS INVOLVED A one-person crusade isn’t going to change your local union, and it isn’t what the union needs. You need teammates and helpers if you want to accomplish long-term change. “Every day you need to ask yourself, ‘Who did I talk to today?’” says Vance Smith of Teamsters Local 135 in Indianapolis. “Get out in the field and have one-on-one, personal conversations.” Have realistic expectations. Not every member is going to want to become as active as you are. If someone wants to get involved, start them off with small jobs first, like talking to you about problems where they work or introducing you to other members. Thank them for their efforts and let them know their work is valuable. “In every workplace, workers show a range of knowledge about and interest in the union, from A to Z,” says longtime organizer Joe Fahey. Don’t try to move people from A to Z immediately—instead, move them from A to B, and so on. Once they’ve gotten their feet wet, ask them to do bigger jobs, like passing out a leaflet or standing with you in the parking lot while you do that. Give them options. Remember, people’s lives are complicated. If someone doesn’t want to get involved at first, don’t write them off. Stay in contact and ask them again later. You’re building a network here, so cast as wide a net as you can. People can surprise you. The more members you have working with you, the more work you can get done. Especially in a local that represents multiple workplaces or industries, getting lots of members involved in your campaign can be critical. Is It Working? Here are some of the ways you can tell your organizing is having an effect: More members are involved in a passive way, like reading a leaflet. More members are taking a small action step, like wearing a button or signing a petition. Some members are taking on organizing tasks, like passing out flyers or making phone calls. Some members are becoming leaders and taking initiative. If these things aren’t happening, take a step back and re-evaluate your strategy. Are you doing too much yourself? Do you need to reach out to more departments? Do you have the right message? This advice is drawn from the Labor Notes book Democracy Is Power by Mike Parker and Martha Gruelle. This article is excerpted from Running for Local Union Office: A Labor Notes Guide. Order the book ($20) and find resources including how to be effective at union meetings, a list of labor education programs, and more at labornotes.org/runningforoffice .

articles.title: Do Peasants Hold the Key to Humanity’s Future?
articles.author: Daniel Colligan
articles.content: In 1966, the sociologist Teodor Shanin boldly asserted that “peasants are the majority of mankind.” This declaration coincided with the beginning of a decades-long increase in academic focus on the peasantry, which, in addition to its demographic weight, was the driving force of some of the most important political movements of the twentieth century. Classic works such as anthropologist Eric Wolf’s 1969 Peasant Wars of the Twentieth Century chronicled the various ways in which subsistence farmers asserted themselves on the world stage. In the sixty years since Shanin made that declaration, the situation of world agriculture has changed dramatically. On large farms, highly mechanized operations have raised productivity and output to unprecedented levels. Smallholder agriculture has been transformed by the adoption of Green Revolution technologies such as synthetic fertilizer, high-yielding crop varieties, and pesticides. A continuous flow of migrants exiting agriculture has swelled the urban areas of both rich and poor countries alike. The epic overhaul of the global countryside has caused the peasantry to recede as an object of interest. Historian Eric Hobsbawm ’s assessment that the twentieth century witnessed the “death of the peasantry” is often taken as a final judgment on the peasantry’s political relevance. That epitaph was reiterated two years ago in the most recent work on (European) peasants targeted at a general audience. A new book attempts to counter this conventional wisdom on the peasantry by arguing that reports of the peasantry’s death have been greatly exaggerated. Maryam Aslany’s Peasants: Makers of the Modern World insists that there are actually more peasants living now than at any point in history: two billion who produce a third of the world’s food. Drawing on her fieldwork in India, Cambodia, Peru, and Ghana, Aslany attempts to “restore to the countryside the visibility it demands.” And the visibility it demands is, in her view, superlative. In an article previewing the arguments of the book, Aslany argues that the present crisis of the peasantry is “the most important story of the 21st century.” Aslany believes peasants to be a supremely important topic, because she thinks these agriculturalists are humanity’s final defense against total ecological ruin. Peasant cosmology’s sacral reverence for nature and peasants’ unique capability to steward natural resources, she claims, provide “our last protection against environmental collapse.” The peasantry’s eco-preserving essence is under continuous attack from urban-based and purportedly progressive forces that do not appreciate the indispensable role peasants play in environmental conservation. Humanity’s survival, then, depends on a global shift in agricultural policy toward supporting and strengthening the peasantry. This is all the more true, in her view, because intolerable urban conditions must lead to future repeasantization. But Aslany’s revisionist perspective on the peasantry suffers from critical flaws. Her misleading historical account of global economic development confounds the role of both states and peasants in it. These distortions lead her to erroneously inflate the peasantry’s potential future importance. Ultimately, her peasant exceptionalism is unconvincing: it is highly doubtful that peasants possess a unique solution to the world’s environmental dilemmas. What Is a Peasant? Where does the two billion peasants figure come from? The source that Aslany cites for her claim regarding the existence of two billion peasants is her article, where she makes a slightly different claim — namely, that the rural populations of the three less-developed continents comprise two billion people: “By my calculations, as many as 2 billion people live in the countryside of Africa, Latin America and Asia, where small family farms dominate.” The article itself does not give any sense of how this particular statistic was derived, but two billion is in line with other estimates of the number of people involved in smallholder agriculture globally. Nevertheless, peasants, smallholder agriculturalists, and rural dwellers are overlapping but distinct categories whose differences should be preserved. Defining peasants is a controversial endeavor. Aslany’s definition of a peasant — “a smallholder farmer who lives off the land . . . relies mainly on family labour, and farms both for subsistence and for the market” — blurs the distinction between farmers who primarily produce for exchange and those who are not fundamentally dependent on markets for their survival. This move allows her to to include a larger swath of people in her study, beyond only those rustics who raise crops and animals primarily for their own family’s consumption. In fact, the cultivators Aslany studies are often highly dependent on markets, either on the input side, to purchase seed, fertilizer, and chemicals, sometimes via financial markets, and/or on the output side, through income generated by sale of their produce. They often cannot subsist on their own produce since they are husbanding nonstaple crops (e.g., coca, cocoa, or sugar). Farming is not even the main income generator for some of the people Aslany profiles. One Cambodian farming couple’s income is overwhelmingly provided through the remittances generated by their children working in South Korean factories. Another farmer, this one in India, holds onto his land only though revenue earned from a transport business. The point here is not to argue for one or another sociological definition of the peasantry or attempt the near-impossible task of precisely enumerating how many people fit any such definition worldwide. Rather, it is to note that a less expansive conception of what a peasant is would lead to an estimate of the peasantry’s size significantly lower than her marquee two billion figure. Repeasantization? Part of Aslany’s desire to stress the continuing importance of the peasantry derives from what she considers the failure of cities and industry to provide a tolerable existence for the future of humanity. The increase in world population over the next several decades will, she predicts, see many return from cities to rural areas and agricultural activities: “When all else fails, land is the only thing; in this sense, peasant cultivation must have a significant role to play in securing humanity’s future.” Aslany tries to buttress this prediction by arguing against the veracity of two “compelling — if unexamined — stories about [the peasantry’s] demise.” The first is that peasant agriculture will decline in tandem with the progress of industry, and the second is that cities will absorb the peasants departing the countryside. Since these are precisely the processes that the world has witnessed over the past century, readers may be perplexed when encountering Aslany’s pushback on these claims. Aslany attempts to rescue the first contention by writing that predictions of peasant agriculture’s demise was an “based on an extrapolation from the highly specific experience of north-western Europe” and “has still not happened.” But depeasantization is a phenomenon that has advanced far beyond the borders of the richest countries. For instance, taking as a sample the countries that Wolf profiles in Peasant Wars — Mexico, Russia, China, Vietnam, Algeria, and Cuba — the International Labour Organization reports the share of labor working in agriculture as under 10 percent in Algeria and Russia, under 20 percent in Cuba and Mexico, and, in China (22 percent) and Vietnam (25 percent), it is half of what it was mere decades ago. The countries Aslany visits in her book generally have higher labor shares in agriculture, but even they have come down rapidly in the twenty-first century: Cambodia’s, for instance, fell from 73 percent in the year 2000 to 33 percent in 2025. On the second claim, Aslany recognizes that some formerly peasant countries like China have seen tremendous rural-to-urban migration. But, she insists, “China is exceptional: it cannot become the general condition.” Again, the data intrudes on this perspective. United Nations figures show the Peasant Wars group with all non-Chinese countries at over 75 percent urbanization, with the exception of Vietnam, which has doubled its urbanization rate to 39 percent in the past generation. The countries Aslany visited, too, exhibit secular trends toward urbanization. In fact, of the three continents Aslany mentions as having significant rural populations, only in Africa is the rural population growing absolutely (although less rapidly than the urban population on the continent). Latin America ’s and Asia ’s rural populations have seen slight absolute declines over the twenty-first century. It is therefore difficult not to be skeptical about Aslany’s predictions of saturated cities producing a demographic movement to the countryside; her statement that “even Europe is seeing traces of what some experts call ‘re-peasantization’” is baffling. It is true that legitimate questions remain about how burgeoning urban populations in less-developed countries will be absorbed into the labor force, especially given that many of these countries are experiencing “ premature deindustrialization .” However, outside of some massive crisis of urban life above and beyond what is currently being experienced in Global South cities, in all likelihood current trends of depeasantization and rural-to-urban migration will continue into the near future. The State as Villain (Marx in Supporting Role) The sense that peasants are currently facing an existential crisis (despite a somewhat contradictory insistence on their endurance) provides the motivating drama for Aslany’s book. Peasants themselves, Aslany avers, are not responsible for their endangerment. Rather, that is the fault of the states that have persecuted them over the last century: “Peasants are in crisis today not because they are somehow unsuited to modern conditions but because they have been hunted to the limits of possibility.” In this “class war between humanity’s urban and rural factions,” deliberate anti-peasant efforts by states have driven many peasants off of their land and threaten to eliminate the peasantry as a category in years to come. The underlying reason that states have hit upon these anti-peasant policies, Aslany contends, is primarily ideological. Drawing on the English example, in which a vanquished peasantry coincided with rapid economic growth, the world’s technocrats adopted this experience as an ideal and, aided by British imperialism, exported it to the rest of the world. Thus, Aslany writes, “The world’s managers have believed their own urban fairy tale: that the peasantry no longer exists – or that it should, in the interests of ‘progress,’ cease to do so.” Chief among the ideologists was Karl Marx, “who did the most to convert the dying peasant of bourgeois fantasy into scientific ‘fact.’” This peasant-averse ideology reached its most grotesque expression in various episodes of the twentieth century, when Marxist-influenced governments, through collectivization or otherwise, waged lethal mass campaigns against the peasantry. This is a radical reinterpretation of the motives of state managers in the past centuries of global economic development, which completely neglects the more straightforward reasons that they pursued policies that did not prioritize peasant interests. State managers’ aspirations to increase economic prosperity derived primarily from the political pressures they faced both domestically and internationally. Domestically, populations clamored for increasing living standards, and businesses demanded assistance in competing with foreign goods. Internationally, state managers wanted to avoid being dominated economically and/or militarily by rival states. Any successful historical example of rapid national economic development has required a transition of the labor force out of agriculture and into services and, especially, industry. While not ignoring the suffering that peasants faced in historical episodes of persecution, it is also true that peasants themselves have found many reasons to voluntarily leave the country for the city. Urban wages are often higher than agricultural ones, and, for many, backbreaking labor in the fields is less preferable than employment in a factory or an office. Cities offer a more exciting cultural life and an escape from rural social conservatism and patriarchal family structures. Not every peasant who left their farm for the city over the past centuries was marched off at gunpoint by the state; migratory flows from countryside to city have existed both in times of acute crisis and in times of relative stability. Therefore, it is misleading to portray depeasantization as a wholly top-down enterprise devised by sinister state bureaucrats drunk on Marxism or modernization theory. Many peasants have voluntarily chosen, for various reasons, to take their chances in the uncertain city rather than on the familiar farm. The Thin Green Line The book’s ultimate argument for the importance of the peasantry lies in peasants’ ecological sensibilities. “The fact that a substantial proportion of the world’s cultivable land is controlled by peasants,” Aslany writes, “protects us enormously against the final exhaustion of natural systems.” Peasants’ sacral veneration of their land and environment, Aslany argues, is actually superior as a form of conservation compared to more conventional legal approaches: “Over prolonged periods, the sacred offers a much stronger form of environmental protection than the law.” Peasant cosmology amounts to a kind of Thin Green Line preventing the world from tipping over into environmental catastrophe. The balance sheet of the peasantry’s relation to the environment, however, is not exclusively on the side of conservation; peasants can play a very damaging ecological role. Smallholder agriculture requires land, which excludes the land from serving other purposes. The more small farms propagate, the more deforestation and biodiversity loss might result. On an individual level, too, small farmers are often compelled to adopt the latest potentially ecologically-damaging cultivation practices, whether it is synthetic fertilizer, pesticide and herbicide use, or others. In the extreme case, as Aslany documents in Ghana , small farmers might opt to despoil their plots with what is euphemistically called “artisanal and small-scale mining,” overwhelming a once-viable farm with toxic waste from gold extraction. In truth, peasant agriculture is not inherently ecologically superior to other forms of agriculture — or, for that matter, other forms of economic activity. Agriculture undoubtedly has an important place in any plan for environmental sustainability. But comprehensive solutions to the climate crisis (to mention just one pressing ecological challenge) must go far beyond the areas where peasants purportedly have expertise. Transitioning to renewable energy sources, for instance, and decarbonizing industry and transit are necessary components of a climate strategy on which peasant cosmology will have very little bearing. All the more reason to abandon notions of peasant exceptionalism when thinking about how to achieve our ecological goals. To the extent that Aslany has a political program in mind to address smallholder agriculture, she advocates placating the farmers who “would love a bit more capitalism in their lives” by deregulating state-sponsored commodity monopolies. But hers is not simply a laissez-faire program. Aslany also urges state support for “iron-clad protection for [peasant] land,” “forms of credit that are quite different from other kinds of businesses,” and “protection from excessive price fluctuations, or downward pressure applied by powerful buyers.” At base, the political program she outlines is one of subsidizing smallholder agriculture rather than an ecologically driven project per se. Perhaps this could be a small component part of a larger ecological strategy, but handouts to small agrarian businesses does not seem like a route to averting climate disaster. Makers of a Previous World Peasants raises pressing questions about agriculture, urbanization, migration, ecology, and economic development, particularly in the Global South. The stubbornly persistent absolute number of people involved in smallholder agriculture is certainly an important phenomenon that must be grappled with in both national and international contexts. But such an assessment is not aided by mangling the history and present of the peasant predicament. Peasants have not left their land over the past few centuries exclusively because they were victims of state persecution. And states have not undertaken industrialization programs only or primarily out of ideological anti-peasant animus. Rather, peasant attraction to cities and new forms of employment provided reason enough for many to migrate. It seems highly unlikely that present trends of urbanization and deagrarianization will sharply reverse in the decades to come. Finally, peasants do not possess a privileged position when it comes to formulating a comprehensive solution to the planet’s environmental crises. Peasants can be said to be “makers of the modern world” only in the sense that in the preceding epoch they provided the demographic foundation for agrarian empires. Today they account for an ever-dwindling share of the world’s population, a minority of global food production, and only really survive in the least developed countries. Extrapolating into the future, repeasantization on a significant scale looks far less likely than absolute peasant numbers dwindling further with the continuing advance of capitalism and falling fertility rates. Karl Marx is often criticized, including by Aslany, for proclaiming that “The country that is more developed industrially only shows, to the less developed, the image of its own future.” However, insofar as this premonition is read as sketching the broad historical arc of depeasantization and urbanization, it hews closer to developments across the subsequent centuries than his critics might care to admit. articles.title: A History of Taxing the Rich in California
articles.author: Fred Glass
articles.content: In the wake of the defeat of Proposition 40, the billionaire tax in California, observers are parsing the loss. The good news is that there were actually two progressive tax ballot measures before the Golden State’s electorate this year, and while we lost Prop 40, we won the other one, Prop 3. This point is key, because it’s not possible to grasp the reasons for the loss of 40 without knowing its intertwined history with Prop 3. Since economic inequality will not be disappearing any time soon, and taxing the rich is an integral aspect of fixing the problem, we need to devise a balance sheet of lessons drawn from these two campaigns to inform the next round. Prop 3 has made permanent a temporary state income tax in place since 2012 on the top 2 percent of income earners. These are people who make at least $370,000 per year. Prop 3 mostly supports public education but also supports other state-funded services. Last year, it brought in over $14 billion in revenue, close to 6 percent of the entire state budget. Prop 3 passed by a comfortable margin of better than 60–40 percent. Prop 40 — which lost 52–48 percent — proposed to tax California’s 250 billionaires on their bloated collective wealth (an estimated $2.4 trillion), a 5 percent levy to backfill cuts that Donald Trump and the Republican Congress made to federal Medicaid assistance to the states. Until now, California’s share came to $20 billion a year. Starting January 1, 2027, the loss of Prop 40 means that unless the state’s governor and legislature come up with a Plan B (and there is barely a glimmer of one at the moment), three million of the poorest Californians will lose access to health care. This goal of Prop 40, to save health care for the state’s indigent, was lost in mainstream media reportage on the campaign, which breathlessly — and in the worst tradition of fawning celebrity journalism — focused on the astronomical sums of money spent against Prop 40 and narcissistic wounds suffered by the ultrarich at the prospect of paying higher taxes. Example: a New York Times story in the final weekend of the campaign, “Inside the War Against California’s Wealth Tax,” managed to spill ink across two pages without saying a single word about the purpose of the tax that the self-absorbed right-wing billionaires were fighting. Little attention, too, was devoted to analyzing what the enormous spigot of political action committee (PAC) money against the billionaire tax purchased: a torrent of some of the most deceptive and deliberately confusing paid messaging ever delivered in a state ballot measure campaign (and that’s saying something). Prop 3, by contrast, received generally favorable coverage and flew mostly below the radar, while Prop 40 was being carpet-bombed. What accounted for the differing treatment? And does the result mean Prop 40 was a first step toward wealth taxes from which we can draw valuable insights and move forward? Or a serious mistake from which it will take a while to recover? What They’re Saying One postelection refrain is the assertion that the billionaires have way too much money and will spend so much (which they won’t even feel) that the people don’t stand a chance to tax the rich. The implication is that progressive forces should work on other issues that we can actually win. There is an obvious element of truth here, but it’s only part of the story. It’s also the defeatist lesson the billionaires would like us to internalize. A more nuanced narrative: Forget a wealth tax. Proposition 3, a top tier income tax, was on the same ballot and won. Only income taxes on the rich stand a chance. Again, a partial truth: the failure of one wealth tax doesn’t mean all will fail. But the devil is in the details. And income taxes on the superwealthy, as Thomas Piketty pointed out a dozen years ago, are so twentieth century. They are still necessary, but they are a mismatch with the ability of the rich to avoid tax scrutiny. And that focus ignores the big enchilada of where the real money is. Then there’s Governor Gavin Newsom’s self-serving mantra: You can’t do it in one state. It has to be a federal wealth tax. Which is half right — we do need that. But it’s not an either/or. Fully one-quarter of the country’s billionaires reside in California, and there’s plenty of need for a fair share of their taxes right here. Finally, for people closer to the labor campaigns for 3 and 40 — they were both led by unions — and tuned into the inside baseball, there are competing stories about why the campaigns did not work together, and crucially, why a handful of important labor and nominally progressive organizations opposed the billionaire tax. The division inflicted real damage on 40 and, with its defeat, perceptions of what’s possible along these lines in the future. Sorting through these viewpoints and explanations with the goal of doing better next time requires some background in California’s tax wars, beginning with the disastrous Prop 13. Had the major backer of the Prop 40 campaign, SEIU-United Healthcare Workers, absorbed the history and applied its lessons from the outset, things might have gone differently. That knowledge might have also given the leadership of the Prop 3 campaign a more expansive view of the state’s tax needs than the narrow picture they felt compelled to defend. Prop 13 No examination of California’s tax politics can avoid the legacy of Prop 13. The proposition was placed on the California ballot in 1978 by the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, an anti-tax group backed by big business. It turned out to be a small government, anti-tax program replicated by the Right all across the United States. Prop 13 capped property taxes at 1 percent of assessed value and limited increases in tax rates to no more than 2 percent per year. Although it was sold to the public in a time of high inflation as a measure to “keep grandma in her home” on her fixed income, it applied to both residential and commercial property. This meant, over time, that large commercial property owners would pocket billions of dollars in the difference between what they pay in taxes and what they would be paying if their property, increasing in value over the years, was reassessed upward to market value. Prop 13 didn’t stop with revisions to the property tax code. A state constitutional amendment, it changed the threshold for the legislature to pass any tax from a simple majority to two-thirds supermajority, and the same for local taxes. Meanwhile, it left a simple majority in place for reducing or eliminating a tax. It mandated that property value reassessments to current market rate could only take place when the property was sold, and even then, with loopholes that allowed corporations to avoid reassessment and thus higher taxes. Beyond the details of its mandates, two other facets of the measure bear mention. Its dog-whistle racist campaign message pitted white homeowners against renters and welfare recipients: as in, “Your hard-earned tax dollars shouldn’t be wasted on black and brown poor people” — a template for conservative campaigners elsewhere. It represented a backlash, in a time of high inflation, against the last gasps of social movements of the 1960s and ’70s, especially the gains of the civil rights movement and rise of public sector unions. Prop 13 was a traumatic event from which consultants and politicians couldn’t recover for more than three decades, preventing them from understanding that yes, it was actually still possible to tax the rich. What began as a political defeat morphed into a self-inflicted inhibition and common sense. Lesson One: Don’t Forget About the Money The first progressive tax campaign I worked on was in 1992. A combination of upper-tier personal income and corporate tax increases, Prop 167 was placed on the California state ballot by public sector unions seeking to draw business contributions away from support of Republican Governor Pete Wilson’s ballot-box attempt to concentrate power over the state budget into his office. It was the first effort in a decade and a half to tax the rich following passage of Prop 13 but, still suffering below its shadow, the plan was not completely serious. After raising the money to get the tax on the ballot, the unions directed staff like me — I was communications director for the California Federation of Teachers (CFT) at the time — to work the campaign but spent no money on media. Meanwhile, business interests treated the threat seriously, put together a war chest, and expended millions on media buys. California Governor Pete Wilson with then-President George H. W. Bush. (Records of the White House Photograph Office / George H. W. Bush Presidential Photographs) Yet until three weeks before Election Day, the two sides were polling dead even. At that point, the anti-tax forces pulled out all the stops. You could not turn on a radio or TV without teeth-gnashing boutique owners sobbing about how they were going to lose the businesses they had built with their own two hands. Ultimately, the business coalition outspent the unions by a margin of more than twenty to one. In actuality, no small businesses would have been affected by the taxes. But the tactic of corporations hiding behind mom-and-pop stores, deployed against progressive taxes since time immemorial, proved effective. That prevarication, coupled with the equally venerable blackmailing canard that all the “job creators” would leave the state — and multiplied by the huge imbalance in political spending — meant that we lost by a wide margin, 59–41. All the smart people said, “You see. We told you. California is an anti-tax state and will remain that way forever.” Some of us felt the story had a different moral. Studying the campaign timeline, we saw that progressive taxes were at first blush popular. Until the opposition’s river of negative media advertising widened into a flood, with no comparable answer forthcoming from our side, the public was far from convinced how evil Prop 167 was. We posited that if the unions were to pony up a reasonable amount of campaign funding for media alongside a robust field operation, we could win a future campaign. But that insight — blocked by the common wisdom among the political cognoscenti that California’s electorate had been “anti-tax” since Prop 13 and would remain that way until Judgment Day had to wait for some twenty years to be tested. Poor consolation: the unions’ feint worked, and Wilson’s measure went down to defeat. Lesson Two: The Right Message at the Right Time Two decades later, following the subprime mortgage housing crash and Great Recession, my union organized and led a successful campaign to pass a progressive tax. After three years of massive state budget cuts pummeling public schools and social services, the state still faced a record multibillion-dollar budget deficit. To ward off further harm, we went on offense, pulling together a coalition that included unions and community and faith-based groups. In our early meetings we came up with three criteria to test in opinion research: What tax would raise the largest amount of revenue, drawn from the most progressive source, with the best chance of winning? These deliberations and tests resulted in our proposal for a millionaire tax ballot measure to add two top-tier marginal tax rates to the state income tax schedule: an additional 3 percent on income between $1 million and $2 million, and 5 percent on any income above $2 million. We calculated that this would raise $5 billion — not enough to fill the entire state budget hole, but a good start and, following our criteria, winnable. The core of our message: “Tax the rich for schools and services.” We had tested similar sentiments a year earlier with a march from Bakersfield to Sacramento and found over six weeks that they resonated deeply in the communities of the central valley, supposedly a conservative bastion. Reinforced now by our opinion research, we began circulating petitions to gather the requisite number of voter signatures to place our millionaire tax on the ballot. Then-Governor Jerry Brown had a different idea. Notoriously averse to opinion research, and with a record of electoral success based on his gut instincts, he rejected our overtures to join the campaign and put a rival petition for signatures into circulation with a mix of progressive and regressive taxes, including increases on the lowest income earners along with a 1¢ sales tax increase. Our research told us (and we told him) that this would not fly with the electorate. Jerry Brown campaigns in 2010. (Bob Tilden / CC BY 2.0 ) Our proposed measure came out on top of his in five straight opinion polls over several months, but he remained unmoved until the first week of March 2012. During that interval, he shaved away the other unions in our coalition with a razor governors have at their disposal: the threat to veto any legislation sponsored by groups that refused to comply with his will. Despite the loss of these partners (who behind the scenes let us know their hearts were still with us), we retained sufficient resources and coalition partners to put ten thousand marchers carrying millionaire tax signs in the streets of the capital, parading past Brown’s windows. Two days later, we announced the results of a new poll showing our numbers going up and his going down. Brown finally caved. He called CFT president Joshua Pechthalt, a high school social studies teacher in Los Angeles, and worked out a compromise deal. This became Proposition 30, with two parts: three tiers of additional 1 percent tax bumps on individuals making $250,000, $300,000 and $500,000 a year, coupled with a modest 0.25 percent sales tax. Brown insisted on inclusion of the latter (we negotiated it down from his original 1¢ sales tax) due to his agreement with the Chamber of Commerce that they would stay out of the fight so long as Brown didn’t “demonize the rich.” With the sales tax, he said, everyone had skin in the game. We didn’t like the sales tax, nor that the Prop 30 tax would be temporary; our millionaire tax proposal had been for a permanent tax. But Brown agreed to limit the sales tax to four years and extend the progressive income tax to seven years. And the Prop 30 package was actually projected to raise more money than our millionaire tax (and it has). Lesson Three: A Big Coalition With Brown on board, and all of our former coalition partners returned to the fold, we were set up for success. But first we had to overcome a messaging hiccup. The governor had been campaigning mostly on the idea that Prop 30 would save education from further cuts. We agreed with that message, but based on our research — and the post–Occupy Wall Street injection of economic inequality into public conversation — we knew that there also had to be a strong emphasis on taxing the rich. Brown’s hodgepodge approach — save education, tear down the state’s wall of debt, shared sacrifice, and reluctantly, fair taxes — had to be redirected to what we knew were the winning messages. After some internal conversations, he dropped the distracting mishmash and became a disciplined messenger, going straight to stripped-down messages on education, fair share of taxes for the rich, and emphasizing that the sales tax (our biggest worry) represented just one tiny penny on a four-dollar sandwich. Prop 30 made it across the finish line with votes to spare, 55–45 percent, overcoming more than $50 million in opposition spending and decades of formerly unshakeable warnings that California voters would never ever vote for a tax. Thanks to Brown’s hefty campaign fund, we slightly outspent the rich conservatives who bankrolled the other side. That, plus our robust ground game (door-to-door canvassing and earned media from demonstrations, town halls, and other public events) and late course correction on messaging made the difference. Prop 30 was the largest income tax increase on wealthy Californians since World War II. Four years later, as the sales tax expired, the coalition brought Prop 55 to the voters to extend Prop 30, this time as a pure progressive tax for another fourteen years. Brown didn’t bother participating, nor did we need him, as the wealthy reactionaries, having had their butts handed to them four years before, stayed home. A unified labor movement, with adequate funding and support from a wide spectrum of progressive community partners, executed well, and Prop 55 won in a landslide, by 64–36, demonstrating the popularity of taxing the rich if an undisturbed electorate makes its choice without a thumb on the scale from a well-heeled opposition. The above are key pieces of the ancestry to this year’s Proposition 3 victory, which made the Prop 55 tax permanent. But there’s one more election story we should review, the lessons of which help explain Prop 3’s success and the defeat of Prop 40 on November 3. Split Roll In March 2020, now retired, and prey to the notion that “idle hands are the devil’s workshop”, I was gathering signatures with my local faculty union for the “Schools and Communities First” ballot measure, ultimately Prop 15. Generated by the same progressive tax coalition behind Props 30 and 55, Prop 15 was the long-anticipated “split roll” tax meant to overcome the choke hold placed over the state budget via property tax limitations in 1978’s Prop 13. Prop 15 proposed a simple change: resetting the tax basis of commercial property from its last purchase price to current market value. It explicitly excluded residential and agricultural property and, attempting to neutralize small business opposition, set the bar for reassessment to property worth $3 million or more. It would have drawn more than 90 percent of its revenues from less than 10 percent of commercial property holders — entities like Disney and Chevron whose owners paid property taxes based on long-past-shelf-life assessments, robbing the state and its public services of billions of dollars each year. At the outset, the measure polled well, although not as strongly as the millionaire tax had. But it ran into three problems. The broad labor/community progressive tax coalition, well prepared, had gathered the most signatures ever for a California ballot measure campaign — 1.7 million — by mid-March. It would have been even more, but the intervention of the COVID-19 pandemic put a premature end to that activity. As it turned out, this represented but the beginning of how the pandemic undercut the yes campaign. With the imposition of restrictions on public events and face-to-face contact, one of the main tools of labor-community coalitions against big money, grassroots people power, largely evaporated. Door-to-door canvassing and large rallies to draw earned media were out, as was tabling and leafleting in public spaces. The campaign thus developed a decent virtual speakers bureau program, including relational organizing efforts and battalions of letter-to-the-editor writers. Although Prop 15 phone banking was well staffed with volunteers, it became tough for voters to distinguish volunteers from paid callers funded by oil corporations, realtors, and large commercial property owners like Chevron. Already weeks before Election Day, phone banks had been rendered less effective due to voter fatigue at the tsunami of calls. A second factor was the problematic role of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP). Its president, Alice Huffman, steered the state organization into a no endorsement on the campaign, while her political consulting firm was accepting $740,000 in No on 15 contributions. The Huffman-led NAACP’s endorsement figured prominently in the massive direct mail operation that sent deceptive “No on 15” literature streaming into African American households, which claimed falsely that 15 would tax homeowners. The NAACP position was partly countered by Prop 15 endorsements from other institutional pillars of black communities, but it sowed confusion among African American voters. Current California Governor Gavin Newsom speaks at the California Economic Summit in 2019. (Government of California) Third, Governor Gavin Newsom endorsed the measure late and declined to campaign for it. By contrast, Jerry Brown had been out every day in October 2012 calling for the passage of Proposition 30. Governors are reliable media magnets. The no side outspent the pro-15 forces by some $20 million, most of which went to TV advertising. Newsom missing in action meant the loss of earned media opportunities that could have counterbalanced the negative ads. Had any one of these factors gone the other way, Prop 15 would have won despite its funding disadvantage. Instead, it lost narrowly, 52–48. Between Election Campaigns The defeat of Prop 15 and the pandemic in which it occurred left a nasty dent in progressive tax work and on the general atmosphere of the political left in California. The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) played a significant role in the Prop 15 campaign, mounting a coordinated statewide effort among its twenty chapters. Its activists, fresh from the 2020 Bernie Sanders primary victory over Joe Biden in the state, had regrouped after Biden clinched the nomination and enthusiastically staffed phone banks for 15, logging more calls than most unions. But after November, the two major political disappointments in a nine-month span sent the mostly youthful cohort into a demoralized space; membership and activism decayed over the next few years. A similar dysphoria enveloped the rest of the progressive tax coalition, which largely lost momentum, nursing its wounds through the 2024 election cycle. Beyond the general disorientation and social anomie fostered by the pandemic, the education unions (the California Teachers Association [CTA], CFT, and significant sectors of the Service Employees International Union) leading the coalition had to face unrelenting attacks from the Right for their support of school closures, diluting energy for other commitments. One of the coalition’s community organizations, California Calls, kept the faith and continued to host sparsely attended meetings. Only CFT, with little active support from the other groups, pushed a new effort in the legislature. The union worked with Alex Lee, a state assemblymember in Alameda and Santa Clara counties (and the only state representative at the time associated with DSA) to promote wealth tax legislation. Since everyone understood Newsom would veto any such bills, a paper Democratic legislative supermajority meant nothing (even if it had been unified on the issue, which it wasn’t) and these bills did not advance. Limited meetings and deferred decision-making brought no campaign in 2024. But heading toward the 2026 midterms, the coalition got its act together, tested the waters on several proposals, and decided its best move was to make Prop 55 permanent. This would ensure that the funding — an average above $10 billion a year from the progressive tax, or around 5 percent of the entire state budget — would continue, without which the public sector, especially education, would suffer serious budget reductions, and high-end income earners would receive an entirely unnecessary tax cut. Or so went the plan before Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill.” HR 1 gave federal tax cuts to the rich and paid for it with massive reductions to Medicaid, including a loss of some $20 billion a year for California’s share of that program (called “Medi-Cal” here). The looming threat to Medi-Cal and by extension to health care jobs spurred SEIU-United Healthcare Workers into action. Enter the Billionaire Tax A 120,000-member statewide union representing frontline workers across numerous corporate and public health care entities, UHW stood to lose tens of thousands of jobs after January 1, 2027, if nothing changed. Its president, Dave Regan, had used ballot measures in the past — dozens of them — to leverage his union’s interests in Sacramento. Sometimes this meant maintaining the efforts all the way to November,and at other times agreeing to drop them from the ballot if negotiations with employers or the legislature gained improved outcomes. So no one was sure, when the billionaire tax entered the picture in September 2025 with a filing for title and summary, whether it was a straightforward entry into the ballot measure lists or a bargaining ploy for Regan with Gavin Newsom and the state legislature. What unfolded suggests an initial goal of a negotiating chip that, in failing, forced the union, fatefully, to repurpose it as a real ballot campaign. The measure itself, despite claims by opponents that it was poorly designed, was put together by a rock-star team of progressive economists and lawyers who fully understood the present and future perils of nonchalant-ing its construction and, at least from this layman’s point of view, gave it a solid foundation on both economic and legal grounds. Although Regan approached the progressive tax coalition with a request for support, the conversation did not go well. Its leaders felt the measure was ill-timed and could get in the way of Prop 55 renewal. Regan’s position was essentially a pointed question: What about the three million Medi-Cal recipients and thousands of union jobs? To which the coalition leaders gave an unsatisfactory answer predicated on by no means certain budgetary maneuvers and legislative goodwill. Regan’s blunt personality preceded him into the room and was a factor in the discussion, which ended in mutual antagonism. The Opposition Consolidates By late December, several of the wealthiest tech moguls in California, having created the “Building a Better California” PAC to oppose the tax, celebrated the season with a party in Marin whose guests included Sergey Brin (Google cofounder, worth $250 billion and a MAGA donor) and Newsom. Brin reportedly cornered the governor and gave him a piece of his mind about the tax, threatening to leave the state if it passed. Newsom promised to try to get rid of it and was as good as his word, quickly becoming its most high-profile non-right-wing billionaire opponent and reliably delivering their false talking points (all the billionaires will leave, innovation will be smothered, California will be left a smoking husk). As a signal to his left that he didn’t share an entire bed with right-wing sociopaths, he added his own two cents: billionaires do need to pay their fair share, but a) at the federal level, not via the state, and b) it’s a good idea but fatally flawed (repeating a commonly employed argument for campaigns against ballot measures). Google cofounder Sergey Brin poured massive sums into the campaign against Proposition 40. He is pictured here, alongside Elon Musk and Jensen Huang, receiving the National Medal of Science at the Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace on October 8, 2026. (Daniel Torok / The White House) The measure received its title and summary around the first of the year (late for this sort of thing; Prop 3 had been gathering signatures already for months), and UHW began campaigning at the same time as the billionaires and their puppet governor danced and sang before an eager audience of mainstream media editors and reporters — none of whom seemed to know how to ask uber-rich people questions like: What impact will passage of this measure actually have upon your life/finances/business?; What is a greater value, your keeping every penny or millions of poor people keeping access to health care?; What does it mean to “leave the state” when you already own multiple mansions all over the country and world?; or Without your tax dollars, what other action do you suggest the government should take to prevent this health care debacle from occurring? The small coterie of fuming billionaires unearthed and spent the quarters from their couch cushions (piling up close to $400 million to date and counting, the largest sum ever expended on a California ballot initiative) to pay for consulting firms, gather signatures for two poison-pill measures to nullify 40, launch salvos of direct mail. and reserve massive media buys. Regan met with Newsom and attempted to work out a deal. In exchange for the governor’s support, the UHW president offered to pull the measure from the ballot and drop to a new bottom line: from 5 percent to 2 percent. This would have had the effect of reducing the revenue from $100 billion over five years to $40 billion — enough to get through two years of covering the Medi-Cal cuts before (presumably) a Democratic administration would be in national office, which (again presumably) would restore federal funding for Medicaid. But Newsom declined the deal. There matters stood until the June midterm Democratic primary. When Tom Steyer, the sole gubernatorial candidate supporting the billionaire tax, failed to make it into the top two for November, the CTA, State Building Trades Council (BTC), and Planned Parenthood, among others, immediately announced their public opposition to the billionaire tax. CTA was the only organization offering a principled reason for its position. Prop 40 allocated 90 percent of its projected revenues to shoring up Medi-Cal, which violated the state budgetary rules put in place from an earlier voter decision, Prop 98, that mandates 40 percent of the state general fund to public education. CTA’s opposition to the billionaire tax was consistent with their long-standing defense of that line in the sand. If it had stopped there, its hands would have been clean. Instead its leaders signed onto the scary and false messaging flowing from the billionaires’ playbook: Prop 40 would cause the billionaires to flee. The state would lose substantial tax dollars. Because the tax is temporary, voters should reject it, because it doesn’t meet the long-term needs of the state. The last one took the cake, as CTA with its other breath was urging passage of Prop 3, which it had supported as a temporary tax beginning in 2012 up to this election cycle. At the time of CTA’s announcement, it posted its recommendations for the full slate of propositions on its website. Next to the no vote on Prop 40, it placed, without explanation, a link to the Building a Better California website. After a few weeks the link was removed. The public statements from the BTC, Planned Parenthood, and the others simply parroted the billionaires’ talking points and aren’t worth dissecting. It is important to note a common strand among these nominally progressive groups’ decision-making processes: none offered a plebiscite to their members on the question. The BTC is one of the most conservative sectors of the labor movement and reliably tails behind the promises of construction capital for jobs. It was Planned Parenthood’s foundation board, which relies on philanthropy, that voted for opposition. These moves were amplified by the billionaire media machine, which emphasized the split in the progressive community and labor when it wasn’t simply pretending that “teachers” were opposed. (The lie was exposed, to little media notice, when two of the largest local CTA affiliates, United Teachers Los Angeles and United Educators of San Francisco, came out for Prop 40. Shortly afterward the California Federation of Teachers, which had been neutral, and which has a more democratic governance structure than CTA, switched to a support position.) Momentum Returns and Recedes Things looked bad for Prop 40 until three days at the beginning of August. At that point, UHW’s organizing within two of the major institutions of California progressive politics paid off. First, the state Democratic Party leadership, expressing its displeasure with the governor, voted narrowly to endorse the billionaire tax. The next day, with President Lorena Gonzalez leading the charge, the California Federation of Labor Unions came overwhelmingly on board. As icing on the cake, the California Nurses Association joined the newly expanding coalition the following day. But this represented the high point of the campaign. Late endorsements and sporadic earned media emanating from such events as enthusiastic rallies featuring Bernie Sanders and Ro Khanna and cheerleading by Nobel Prize–winning economists turned out to be no match for the record-setting spending tide of the other side, which all along had been steadily eroding the early advantage in poll numbers among a public disgusted with Trump-supporting oligarchs. A no campaign has more messaging tools at its disposal than the pro side of a ballot measure. Where the latter has to make and hold its case before the electorate on the merits, the opposition — especially one with an unlimited pocketbook — doesn’t have to convincingly argue on the same ground. It only needs to cast doubt on the enterprise, showing (or claiming) that various trusted messengers are opposed, rolling out “experts” who “prove” it’s all wrong, and muddling the issues through fearmongering and misdirection. Communications from hell, summoned up by demonic billionaire-backed consultants performed those tasks well. Homeowners learned that they were the target of unnamed but terrifyingly evil “Sacramento politicians” who wanted their homes (like those in the 2020 split roll campaign). Old people found that their pensions were going to be taken away by Prop 40. “Stanford professors” (usually not identified for who they were: the right-wing Hoover Institute) demonstrated that the tax would strip California of innovation and tax revenues. And so on. Progressive tax campaigns produce time-tested, predictable reactions from right-wing rich people, which backers of the measures do well to inoculate against. While modulating with circumstances, they fall into three main themes: The “job creators” will all leave, taking all the jobs with them in their platinum-lined backpacks. The innovation this time around was substituting wealthy “taxpayers” and “tax revenues” for employers and jobs. This is a tax on “you.” This takes two forms: an outright lie making a levy on 250 people into a general tax, and “First they come for the billionaires, then they come for you.” Misdirection: pretending small business owners/homeowners/pensions are the targets, obscuring the point of economic inequality and the tax-dodging of the superrich. Inoculation is possible, but it requires a sufficient timeline before the campaign proper to manufacture the needles and serum and delivery, and sufficient financial resources to pay for it all. With a relatively popular governor actively opposed, and putatively progressive organizations gravely restating the false messages that billionaires couldn’t have convinced the public to believe on their own, the billionaire tax had too big a mountain to climb. A progressive tax campaign needs three things to have a reasonable shot at winning: the right message at the right time; the largest coalition possible; and sufficient cash for at least a modicum of paid advertising to augment its field campaign and earned media against the most well-funded opposition imaginable. Prop 40 had but one out of three, and it wasn’t enough. Compare and contrast with Prop 3’s advantages. Built on a long-standing and extensive coalition of unions and community organizations, with the full backing of the Democratic political establishment (including the governor, who otherwise never met a progressive tax he liked), and with a bank account supported by the biggest labor political contributor (CTA) in the state, and facing virtually no opposition spending, it offered a free lunch to the public (“not a tax increase” — technically true, just maintaining an earlier one) along with its backward, modestly progressive tax messaging (“If it fails, rich people will get a completely unnecessary tax cut”). Prop 3’s victory relied on keeping below the line of fire aimed at Prop 40. It might have been a larger target itself had the billionaire tax not existed. But in that event, as in 2016 with Prop 55, the progressive tax coalition would probably have prevailed anyway, because it was sufficiently prepared and resourced. CTA did not have to hand the billionaires a winning card against a historically justifiable tax on plutocrats for a good cause. Their action dismissed the possibility of a united two-proposition tax the rich campaign that could have provided much-needed consciousness-raising in the electorate about the evils of our New Gilded Age imbalance of wealth and power. Such a dedicated education campaign remains an urgent task. At one level, it’s pointless to second guess what SEIU-UHW might have done differently to get Prop 40 past the third of a billion dollars a couple dozen sociopathic tech oligarchs spent to keep every speck of their hoard and prevent a few million of the poorest Californians from gaining back the health care Trump stole from them. It’s done. But it’s also essential to understand the mistakes that could have been avoided so as to not commit them again the next time around. What’s Next The loss of Prop 40 does not mean the end of progressive tax conflict in California. It’s a battle lost, not the war. We can close this account with a note about the short term and the longer run. It remains to be seen whether the deal originally offered to the UHW will materialize, and budget maneuvers and modest corporate tax increases or loophole closures backed by the legislature and Governor-elect Xavier Becerra will result in enough revenue to reverse the loss of health care for millions of California residents caused by the cruel actions of Trump and the federal government. It’s within the power of the new governor and legislature, if they are committed to it; the tax increases (on income, since thanks to passage of the billionaires’ deceptive Prop 42, wealth taxes are off the table for the time being) will simply require a legislative supermajority of two thirds. If the “blue wave” of November 3 should mean anything to the legislators, it’s that now is the time to act without fear of electoral retribution on that score. Beyond the immediate need to plug the funding gap left by the failure of the billionaire tax, those interested in reversing the stratospheric economic inequality that allows a handful of spoiled oligarchs to thwart what would otherwise be the will of an electoral majority must rise beyond the narrow definition of success of the Prop 3 coalition. Future progressive tax victories cannot depend on an “I win, you lose” mindset between what should be coalition partners. The key here is that all potential interested partners need to get over sectoral myopia and understand the common problem, the common enemy, and common working-class interests. Or, as Martin Luther King Jr noted in another time and place, “The best way to solve any problem, is to remove the cause.” The other side is serious. Are we?
