articles.title: Robot Boss Is Here
articles.author: Z. Waite
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Corrin Kearney had been delivering pizzas for a Domino’s in North Texas for a few months when their store asked them to install a new app on their phone and keep it open during their shift. Soon, Kearney learned the app was tracking and scoring every delivery route they drove, with the results displayed on a leaderboard back at the store for the whole crew to see. The app uses technology from Drivosity, a company that sells what it calls “cutting edge GPS and AI” driver-monitoring to fast-food chains, including Domino’s and Papa John’s. Each trip is scored from 0 to 100 based on factors including acceleration, braking, cornering and speed. According to Kearney, drivers at their store are expected to keep their scores above 85. Anyone below that score is written up by managers and eventually locked out of the Domino’s system. “Drivosity can effectively fire people,” Kearney said. As a driver captain, Kearney has to write up other drivers, even though they have found the app doesn’t recognize the nuance of many real-world situations. Drivers can be penalized for sudden braking to avoid a collision or rapid acceleration to merge on a highway, forcing them to choose between risking an accident or getting points docked, according to Kearney. “It’s infuriating,” Kearney said. “The AI can tell you you haven’t driven well enough and you get fired.” Drivosity also sells coaching and analytics features, including HustleTime®, which measures how fast employees walk from the store to their car, how long they take handing the pizza to a customer and how long they take walking back. In Drivosity’s promotional videos , franchise owners and managers at Domino’s and Papa John’s praise HustleTime®’s ability to track workers in real time down to the second. Stores can “gamify” this, according to the company website , by having workers compete for better scores. Domino’s and Drivosity did not respond to requests for comment. Fast-food companies are increasingly using AI-powered technology to turn worker behavior — how fast you drive, how warmly you greet a customer, how long you spend in the bathroom — into data that can score, rank, discipline and manage employees. To understand how these AI-driven tools are impacting fast-food workers, Capital & Main interviewed over a dozen workers, researchers and labor advocates, who described error-prone technologies being deployed at a rapid pace, without the consent or awareness of staff, even as their pay and promotions are increasingly shaped by AI-enabled monitoring. “They basically use their population of workers as guinea pigs,” Alexandra Mateescu, a researcher at the nonprofit Data & Society, said of the way that fast-food companies are deploying these new tools. In February, Burger King announced that an OpenAI-powered assistant named Patty was being rolled out at about 500 U.S. restaurants, with plans to reach all U.S. stores by the end of 2026. A few weeks later, the tool arrived at the Burger King in Niagara Falls, New York, where Dante Vasquez took drive-thru orders. “It started with a little AI voice in our headset,” said Vasquez. Then the monitoring features started. Each drive-thru conversation was scored on friendliness and upselling, with the numbers displayed on a screen in front of Vasquez as he worked. Anyone could click on a transaction to hear a recording and review the AI-generated transcripts. Green boxes marked what he’d done well — a “Good morning!” or “You rule!” Red boxes marked what Patty counted against him: points off for saying “please hold,” or “um,” or not speaking clearly. Managers watched the scores closely, constantly reminding the crew to stay above the 70% friendliness target, Vasquez said. Workers who scored low were cut from the schedule, he added. Vasquez learned to speak the way that Patty wanted. He got so good at it, that customers started asking if he was a bot. His co-workers nicknamed him “Gemini.” “The system wants me to talk like a robot, so I’m talking like a robot,” Vasquez said. “It just gets so mentally degrading.” Burger King has said publicly that the system was not designed to evaluate individual employees. But Capital & Main reviewed screenshots from a Burger King training module, and images of the dashboard in use, showing individual drive-thru conversations timestamped and marked for tone and upselling. Vasquez, and other Burger King employees, some of whom spoke to Capital & Main on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation, said it was easy to identify and discipline individual employees for low scores. Later, Patty started scoring workers on “warmth,” a metric Vasquez couldn’t make sense of. When he asked his district manager how it was calculated, he recalled, she told him to just talk “like a warm blanket.” According to Vasquez, Patty seemed to penalize his Black co-workers more than others for what the system flagged as “improper tone.” Mayu Tobin-Miyaji, counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center, said that scoring workers on warmth or friendliness is “sort of pseudoscience” and that those tools risk penalizing workers for their accents or disabilities. Asked to respond to these concerns, Kristen Viersen, Burger King’s director of communications, emailed Capital & Main a company statement that said, “We have never before heard any example similar to the questions you raised about team members being penalized based on race, gender, ethnicity or accent.” Burger King declined to answer when asked if the company had tested these features for bias. The new monitoring features were intended “to celebrate great examples of friendly service” and allow managers to coach their team, according to the statement, which also said that Burger King has since disabled both features “for further improvements.” Burger King would not say when the features were disabled, and workers said the monitoring was active through August of this year. Co-workers at Vasquez’s restaurant joked that Vasquez would soon be gone, replaced by Patty entirely, a looming threat that was amplified by a sign in the store that reminded workers that Patty was being trained on every headset conversation. Eventually, the stress just wasn’t worth it. He quit in August. “If Patty wasn’t introduced,” Vasquez said, “I would still be working at Burger King.” While large chains have struck high-profile deals with major AI companies — Yum Brands, which owns Taco Bell, KFC and Habit Burger & Grill, announced last year that it was deploying Nvidia-powered computer vision for “back-of-house labor management through real-time analytics and alerts” — a crowd of smaller vendors sells the same kind of AI monitoring to individual franchisees, with far less visibility. Among the more established vendors is Solink, an Ottawa-based company backed by Goldman Sachs that describes itself as “the leader in AI-driven video intelligence.” It works with franchisees of Domino’s, Burger King, McDonald’s, Jack in the Box, Five Guys and other chains. Related: AI, Surveillance and War: Who Is Emerging Technology Really Serving? Solink’s product documentation describes a video-surveillance system capable of flagging workers who arrive late or leave early, take too long on their breaks, fail to wear a hairnet or the correct uniform, use their phones while on the clock or simply stand idle. The software can layer onto a restaurant’s existing security cameras, and it lets managers type in prompts to find footage of specific behaviors or set up automatic alerts. In a statement, a Solink spokesperson, who declined to be named, said the company’s platform helps businesses “improve operations, sales, safety, and customer experience.” It also stressed that Solink “does not offer identification tools such as biometrics or facial recognition,” and that its terms require customers to comply with the law. Data & Society’s Mateescu said these tools are rarely marketed as worker surveillance. Instead they are sold as “loss prevention” or “workflow management” tools. This language, she said, obscures what the technology actually does “both to employees and to consumers.” While some companies use corporate euphemisms to obscure worker monitoring, others are more direct. MashMore, a new potato-themed fast-food restaurant in Albany, New York, is explicit about its AI use. Using commercially available AI models, its co-founders built an HR chatbot, named Mashy after the store’s mascot, that schedules, scores and ranks all employees. Mashy runs on a stream of data employees generate as they work. Workers clock into routines, complete assigned “quests” and upload photos proving that tasks are completed. In exchange they earn “Mashy points,” which set their level in the restaurant’s ranking system and can determine bonuses and promotions. When co-founder and CEO Andy Gor let Capital & Main interact with the chatbot, it didn’t hesitate about who the employee of the month should be. “Shontia Thomas, and it genuinely isn’t a contest,” the chatbot wrote on a screen that Gor shared with a reporter. Gor said the system would never be used to fire an employee, but the chatbot had created rankings for all workers, including those with the lowest scores. Gor wants to make every routine, cleaning task and customer-service expectation tracked, scored and eventually copied from one location to another, so he can check anything from anywhere. “I’m in China right now,” he said. “I can see that during rush hour they cleaned the table nicely. Today, they pass.” MashMore currently has just one location, but Gor wants to franchise fast. His pitch to investors is that the AI tool can manage employees across dozens of locations. Mashy, Gor said, is “our boss. Basically I’m working for him, too.” Efforts to rein in algorithmic management have mostly stalled at the federal level. In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a package of first-in-the-nation workplace-AI laws on Sept. 30. SB 947, the No Robo Bosses Act, bars employers from relying solely on AI to fire or discipline workers. AB 1883 prohibits tools that use AI to infer an employee’s emotional state or collect “neural data.” SB 951 requires employers to notify workers when AI is behind a mass layoff. Tobin-Miyaji said in an email that the emotion-scoring ban would likely cover a tool like Patty — but that No Robo Bosses could be satisfied by “cursory” human oversight, leaving workers “constantly surveilled and quantified.” Unions could in theory negotiate stricter protections than legislation might afford. In 2023, workers in California won the creation of a Fast Food Council, a state body empowered by law to set wages and weigh in on working conditions across the industry. But despite worker efforts to apply pressure to Gov. Newsom, the council currently lacks a chairperson and has not met for over a year. A spokesperson for the council, Charles Hamilton, told Capital & Main that “AI-powered employee monitoring and surveillance has not been presented to the council as an agenda item.” Some workers have tried to head off the technology before it arrives. Sergio Ceja has worked in the kitchen of an Oakland Burger King for four years. He first heard about Burger King’s AI from his wife, who works at a different location. After her store brought in an AI drive-thru ordering system, she told him, several workers were laid off. When Ceja raised his concerns about AI with his managers, he said they told him it was the owner’s call whether to bring in the new tech. Ceja and his co-workers agreed among themselves that if Patty ever came to their store, they would walk out. So far, it hasn’t. Management told them that they don’t plan to bring it in, but that in the future they may need to in order to lift sales and keep the store from closing. Ceja’s worry wasn’t only about layoffs. It was about the kind of job that would be left if he stayed. “You’ll no longer have a co-worker,” he said through an interpreter. “You’ll have the machine.” Capital & Main

articles.title: Why We Rally for Palestine
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Logan W. Cole The following remarks were made in front of Batavia City Hall at Genesee County DSA’s Rally for Palestine on October 3 rd , 2026. This is a reminder as to why we’re still here as we rally on behalf of the Palestinian people in Batavia today – this has all happened since October of 2023: More than 75,000 Palestinians confirmed killed (but more likely hundreds of thousands); More than 174,000 wounded including the highest per-capita rate of child amputees; More than 1,400 killed (that we know of – the Gaza Health Ministry lacks the infrastructure to fully count such deaths) and more than 5,000 injured since the ostensible “ceasefire” last October; More than 10,000 under rubble ; More than 20,000 children killed ; More than 2 million displaced in Gaza – this is more than 91% of the population; More than 267 out of ~1,000 Palestinian journalists in Gaza killed ( more than 26%); More than 9,000 Palestinian political prisoners detained; and More than 92% of homes have been destroyed in Gaza. We stand with people of Palestine, who continue to experience a genocide committed against them by the state of Israel with the backing of the United States government. There are some actions we can take. We can let our voices be heard, as we are today, and we should continue to do so. We can withhold our vote from those candidates who support the genocide. We can support the BDS (Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions) movement and withhold votes from, and oppose efforts of, those who stifle the speech of those who support BDS. We can stand against, and support the abolition of, Immigration Customs and Enforcement (ICE), who have targeted immigrants like Mahmoud Khalil , Leqaa Kordia , and Rümeysa Öztürk who speak out on behalf of Palestinians – it is one struggle and Batavia, especially with the proposed detention center expansion, is one front in the struggle. It’s not complicated. We can’t stop talking about Gaza. Today, we rally for a permanent, actual ceasefire in Gaza, a halt to all sales of weapons used to commit atrocities against the Palestinian people, and a free Palestine from the Jordan River to the Mediterranean Sea. articles.title: New Colonialism in Latin America
articles.author: Tica Moreno
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. We are living in an era of blatant manipulation, interference, and imperialist aggression against Latin America, and the Brazilian elections were a manifestation of this. At the same time, we are facing both the far right and the empire, with its tech giants. The people’s victory in Brazil had the defense of sovereignty as one of its main pillars: the people affirmed that we are no one’s backyard, understood the implications of Meta’s interference in electoral processes, and more people came to understand the methods of imperialism. There is no doubt that our sovereignty necessarily involves the digital realm, and Lula, having been reelected, is very focused on this agenda. It is more than evident that Artificial Intelligence (AI) is one of the central issues in contemporary geopolitics; the United States responds with tariffs and threats to every attempt to build any level of technological autonomy aimed at digital sovereignty. At this point, fortunately, the debate no longer revolves around whether or not we will use AI. It is about how to navigate this shift into a new technological era, in which data is a new factor of production and digital transformation extends to the state and to life as a whole. How can we build a strategic project capable of breaking the chains of subjugation and dependence that structure our region? The Geopolitics of AI Artificial intelligence is not just any technology. We must understand its scope as a general infrastructure, much like electricity. The United States’ strategy to dominate artificial intelligence is made explicit in analyses of the day-to-day workings of U.S. policy: from documents to statements, from diplomacy to war, encompassing the fusion between the state, the military-industrial complex, and major technology companies, as well as their public and private investments. In Latin America, this analysis must take into account the scope of the U.S. National Security Strategy, which aims to control assets that are strategically vital to the United States. To that end, the empire needs to create obstacles in the economic and technological relations between countries in the region and China. Everything is happening very quickly. In less than a year, the Monroe Doctrine has materialized in the combination of the Shield of the Americas and Pax Silica, a U.S. corporate diplomacy initiative to secure its access to the entire artificial intelligence supply chain. Argentina, Chile, Costa Rica, El Salvador, and Panama are participating in both initiatives, as part of a far-right alignment in the service of the empire. It is clear that the electoral contest in Brazil is part of this international balance of power. Related: Brazil’s Election Won in Streets, Not Just at the Ballot Box On 22 September of this year, the ‘ Joint Declaration on the Defense of Sovereignty in the Hemisphere’—to which Colombia and other countries in the region are also signatories—outlines the convergence of both initiatives. In the name of the fight against ‘narco-terrorism,’ the signatories hand over intelligence, critical minerals, and digital infrastructure to Washington’s coordination efforts, supporting the policy of unilateral sanctions defined by the U.S. U.S. documents indicate the goal of promoting the adoption of U.S. AI systems, hardware, and standards worldwide. They aim to export the entire AI technology stack . This means imposing a comprehensive model, organized in layers that support one another. This stack cannot function without a foundation: the territories where the critical minerals of the digital age (lithium, copper, niobium, rare earth elements), energy, and water are found. The other material layer consists of chips and hardware—the components and servers where these tools are trained and where AI models are run. According to the U.S. standard, this refers to Nvidia’s famous GPUs (which not all countries can acquire). The software runs on top of the hardware. In this case, CUDA—a proprietary programming platform that ties AI training to Nvidia’s ecosystem—runs on Nvidia hardware. Next come the data centers and cloud platforms (from Amazon, Microsoft, and Google), which contain a vast number of servers where the extracted data is stored and processed. There are also data centers that train AI models, and these are the ones that consume the most water and energy. Above these layers are the AI models (such as large language models) and the applications that reach users. All of this, let’s remember, depends on gigantic amounts of data—digital records of nearly everything that is alive and everything humanity has produced. Therefore, the United States export of its AI dependency package depends on the extraction of data from the entire population and the natural resources of Latin American countries—which are responsible for sustaining the foundation of the chain—and in return, they provide us with predefined AI models. This is the model of the Pax Silica, the agreement that guarantees what the White House needs to counter China’s rise, while maintaining Latin America’s subjugation as a supplier of minerals and territories. Related: BRICS Rejects Western Domination Embraces De-Dollarization Paths to Sovereignty In Brazil, the creation of conditions for sovereignty began through mining-related policies, and not necessarily in the digital sphere. Brazil has the world’s second-largest reserve of rare earth elements, but accounts for a tiny fraction of processing. The technology for processing and refining is concentrated almost entirely in China, which also holds the largest reserve of rare earth elements protected by a sovereign policy. The United States depends on Brazilian rare earths and other critical minerals, such as lithium from Bolivia and Argentina, to compete in the AI race. Brazil’s National Policy on Critical Minerals, approved in September 2026, provides for investments to process and refine rare earths domestically and establishes a council—linked to the Office of the President—with the power to veto transfers of control over mining companies. This is a response to the acquisition of the Serra Verde mining company in Goiás by USA Rare Earth, with the backing of the U.S. government. Shortly before that, in August, the Brazilian government had announced the development of a sovereign cloud and AI. The Lula administration’s advances in the area of artificial intelligence sovereignty stem from intensifying geopolitical dynamics. Clearly, there are disputes within the government itself over which path to follow; for a time, a passive and even covert view of sovereignty regarding this technology prevailed, advocating the notion that simply hosting data on national territory would be sufficient for our digital sovereignty. It is worth recalling that there is a law in the U.S. (the Cloud Act) stipulating that data processed in the clouds of U.S. companies falls under that country’s jurisdiction. We start from a position of deep dependence. The Brazilian government has spent billions on digital licenses and services—primarily with Microsoft, Google, and AWS—rather than investing in developing its own capabilities. And that is why the announcements made in August of this year are so important: a 2.3 billion reais investment package in sovereign AI infrastructure, supercomputers, and the development of AI models in Portuguese, in addition to an agreement to establish a 100 percent national cloud. The Brazilian government has finally stated that the development of these technologies must be based on models in which the code belongs to the nation itself. Clearly, these are important steps in a long process fraught with limitations and contradictions. Precisely for this reason, they must be integrated into a strategic project for development, industrialization, and popular sovereignty. Given the pace at which AI is advancing, it does not seem feasible to start from scratch. The race to develop models is becoming increasingly evident due to the progress of China’s open-source models, which also extend to the hardware sector. It is essential to establish the terms of partnerships in AI development, situating each one within the framework of the strategic project to achieve a viable path toward sovereignty. In the case of the supercomputer, the government announced partnerships with the Chinese companies iFlytek and Huawei (which have been sanctioned by the U.S.), establishing terms for technology transfer, the training of 3,000 professionals, and the capacity to lead model development. Obviously, this measure runs counter to U.S. objectives. Related: Lula's Stunning Victory Exposes the Cracks in Trump's Latin American Empire On the path toward building digital sovereignty, Brazil asserts that we need AI models in Portuguese, reflecting the diversity of accents and forms of expression. We already have some, trained using ChatGPT, for example. The imposition of foreign AI leads to homogenization—a cognitive standardization that shapes what questions are asked, how answers are structured, and how images are generated when reconstructing memory and recognition. This also encompasses the debate over what constitutes valid knowledge, training data, the human labor crystallized within AI, and the continuous extraction of data that becomes a means of behavior modulation. An AI trained in Portuguese is a step forward. But it is necessary to channel the sovereign development of AI within the framework of a democratic and popular project for the country. To achieve sovereignty in the realm of AI (and in the digital age), data must be treated as a public good. If we consider data as a factor of production and recognize its central importance to the new quality of the productive forces, ensuring data sovereignty and control is tied to the struggle over the direction of our future as a people—and over our ways of producing and reproducing life. And in that regard, we still have a long way to go. We need to build the capacity to manage data from local communities in a way that serves its people: data related to the healthcare system, biodiversity, the fight against deforestation, or preparedness for the effects of El Niño; agricultural data that contributes to food sovereignty; as well as data on cities and urban mobility. There is also data collected by different government sectors that we still lack the capacity to process and integrate. For example, there has never been so much discussion about violence against women. One technology used as a solution is an electronic ankle monitor for the abuser and an alert system for women, so they know when the abuser is approaching. This keeps women in a constant state of alert and ultimately places the responsibility for protecting themselves squarely on their shoulders. However, the Brazilian government still lacks the capacity to use AI to integrate health and social assistance data in order to develop predictive capabilities that could guide, for example, more preventive policies against violence. In every sector, we can think of examples of what is needed and what can be done, as well as what must be regulated and combated. A sovereign AI is only possible with a democratic and sovereign state. And it must be subject to popular control over what to develop, with what data, and to address what needs of the population: from education to health, from the production of healthy food to ensuring a life free from violence, from work with rights to the right to rest and leisure. Related: Extreme Lawfare and the MAGA Offensive in Latin America Popular movements have argued that the development of AI, as social infrastructure, must be subordinate to a project that guarantees rights and a dignified life—not to increased surveillance and corporate power. On the other hand, fascism—intrinsically misogynistic and racist—gains strength through the AI of the Empire’s major tech corporations. That is the struggle currently being waged in Brazil. Precisely because this is such a unique historical period, the United States will use all its tools to try to subjugate us, just as it does with countries in the region currently governed by the far right or with countries devastated by war. Our historic task is to turn the defense of digital sovereignty into a popular struggle, with concrete advances; to develop the capacity to break free from dependence; and to forge sovereignty at this very moment when the foundations of the new technological era are still up for grabs. Globetrotter

articles.title: Decline of the American Empire
articles.author: Tom Engelhardt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Talk about extreme. Talk about mad. Talk about off the charts. We’re all now, I fear, on the national equivalent of the Six Flags roller coaster from which a man recently fell to his death . Honestly, can you even believe this world of ours? This old guy can’t, I’ll tell you that. Nothing truly prepared me for Donald J. Trump as president of the United States—not once, but twice!—or for the all-too-bizarre world that came with him. (Or did it, in fact, arrive ahead of him and pave the way?) How could I ever have prepared myself for that? I mean, great imperial powers have gone down many, many times before in history, but not, I suspect, quite this way, not by giving that downhill slide the imprint and imprimatur of a genuine maniac as imperial leader. Not by implementing that roller-coaster-style ride with a full-scale nuttiness that, once upon a time, would have been politically beyond imagining in this country. Go ahead, give me another example of such a phenomenon, of a leader like Trump in the history of any great power in decline (and there have certainly been many of those). Personally, I can’t think of one in the last couple of centuries ever being headed by quite the equivalent of You Know Who at just such a moment. And yet, strangely enough, I’ve seen no one say such a thing. Related: Welcome to Trumpworld, Where Political Reality Defies Belief Keep in mind, of course, that Donald Trump is all too emblematic of this world of... well, I’m not sure I can say “ours” anymore. In a way, symbolically speaking, you couldn’t ask for anything more descriptive of our moment than him and the way he’s rejected outright the all-too-obvious state of a planet also going down, down, down in roller-coaster fashion, not if you want to truly grasp what’s happening in this world of ours these days. As he said at the United Nations in 2025, “This ‘climate change,’ it’s the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world, in my opinion. All of these predictions made by the United Nations and many others, often for bad reasons, were wrong. They were made by stupid people that have cost their countries fortunes and given those same countries no chance for success. If you don’t get away from this green scam, your country is going to fail.” Buy the Book Yes, the president of the United States, a remarkable scamster himself, has simply rejected reality as a scam in a way that should be considered historically remarkable, if not unique. Having first done so long ago (calling climate change a Chinese “hoax” as early as 2012), he’s never really stopped. And little harm it did him, it seems. After all, on this distinctly warming planet of ours, he did indeed win a second term in office in 2024. Of course, when the British Empire (or, in fact, any other great imperial power of the past that you want to mention) went down, our planet wasn’t yet on the downhill slope as well. Now, however, it certainly is. (Hey, it’s early November and, here in a distinctly warming New York City , I have yet to don my usual fall jacket even once!) So, perhaps as the leader of what remains the greatest power (or possibly I mean greatest mess of a power) on this planet, Donald Trump will come to be known not as the “hot” president but as the heat president (as he’s making our all-American world ever hotter, whether you’re talking about politics or the weather). He’s even agreed to pay companies to cancel planned wind-power projects And speaking about the (political) weather, it’s true that American voters only recently rejected him in what’s come to be known as a “ blue tsunami “ (though maybe a red Trumpnami would have been more accurate). Still, whatever we voters did in the recent midterm elections, the mad Donald distinctly remains the president of the United States for two more incredible (or do I mean incredulous?) years and that certainly is no small thing. And only recently, he also appointed Stephen Miller as his chief of staff. Yes, we’re talking about the fellow that Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries has termed “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands.” Related: Climate Change Is a Slow-Motion Nuclear War—and We're Already Counting the Dead A Trumpian Heat Tsunami In some fashion, given the recent election, Donald Trump does distinctly seem to be going down, down, down. Unfortunately, he also seems remarkably prepared to do his best in the two years to come to take the rest of us and the planet down with him. And believe me, that’s no small thing. After all, American voters have twice elected a climate-change denier of the first order to the highest office not just in the land but, given American power, in the world. And if you don’t think that’s remarkable, historically (or do I mean futuristically?) speaking, then I wonder what is? Yes, it’s all too obvious that this planet is now going down, down, down, thanks to the continued pouring of fossil fuels into the atmosphere and the distinct overheating of this world of ours. And it’s not exactly complicated what needs to be done in response. Nonharmful energy sources (solar, wind, and hydropower) have to become the heart and soul of human life on this planet. But don’t even dream of such a thing in the universe of Donald J. Trump, who seems intent on nothing less than taking us all (and our children, grandchildren, and great-grandchildren) down with him in what might be thought of as a Trumpian heat tsunami. At the very least, in imperial terms, he’s turning climate change (and so the fate of this planet) over to that other great power of this moment, the rising green power and largest investor in green energy on this planet, China (even if that country also continues to pour more fossil fuels— 35% of the global total —into the atmosphere than any other country). In the meantime, give him the credit he deserves. After all, he is president for the second time of the imperial power that, since World War II, has put more money into its military than so many other countries combined. A possible $1.5 trillion is likely to go into the Pentagon budget alone in 2027 and President Trump has never really stopped fighting (and losing ) wars against far lesser powers. In doing so, he is, believe it or not, following in a great American tradition with the war he launched (with Israel) against Iran that has proven (with the Strait of Hormuz closed ) a global economic catastrophe and undoubtedly helped the Democrats sweep the recent midterm elections. Related: Donald Trump: The President of American Decline For Donald Trump, it seems that there are simply never enough tsunamis on this misbegotten planet of ours and he’s continued to threaten far worse in his war with Iran, saying that he may have to “destroy the rest of the country” (which might, of course, even be a threat, for the first time in more than 80 years, to use atomic weaponry on this planet, though he’s also denied that he would do so). Can there be any question that, two years into his second term in office, he is now taking us (and the rest of the planet) on a roller coaster ride to hell, or do I mean into the trashcan of history? It makes this 82-year-old grandfather sad indeed to imagine the world that “my” president is now preparing (if that’s faintly the word for it) for my grandchildren. They just don’t deserve this, do they? Tom's Substack

articles.title: Reject “Electoralism.” Embrace Socialist Electoral Strategy.
articles.author: Elliot Lewis
articles.content: In elections this year, 169 (and counting) candidates or ballot initiatives endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) nationally or by its chapters succeeded at city, state, and federal levels. DSA member Zohran Mamdani is the mayor of the largest city in the country, and it seems increasingly possible that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will run for president of the United States in 2028. These exciting developments raise the question of the role of elections in the socialist project. Today some on the Left refer to socialists running for office as “electoralism.” But that term has a specific historical meaning, which much of the radical left has long viewed with disdain. It’s worth getting clear on what distinguishes electoralism in that sense from a transformative democratic socialist electoral strategy like the one many in DSA are trying to work toward today. Unlike anarchist or syndicalist approaches to organizing, which view militancy outside of the state as the sole mechanism for bringing about social change, both electoralist and democratic socialist electoral strategies see contesting elections as an important tool for helping bring about socialism. But while electoralism focuses exclusively on winning elections and making change through policy measures, a democratic socialist strategy understands elections and socialist governance as one important means among others of achieving reforms and facilitating the organization of the working class into an agent capable of transforming society. Electoralism and Social Democracy Electoralism has existed nearly as long as the socialist movement itself. In Evolutionary Socialism , published in 1899, German socialist Eduard Bernstein argued that capitalism could be gradually overcome through a peaceful electoral path and piecemeal legislative reform. In the early twentieth century, social democratic parties across Western Europe seemingly began making good on this vision, winning state power through elections and attempting to enact pro-worker reforms. Though most early socialists did not think of themselves as “electoralists” and understood the importance of organizing outside the state, particularly in the workplace, over time social democratic strategy focused more and more on winning elections and parliamentary power. Social democrats eventually became electoralists in practice, if not in name. When social democratic parties were on the rise in the early and mid-twentieth century, the industrial working class was increasingly joining unions and engaging in mass strikes, giving the parties significant political leverage . This combination of power inside and outside the state allowed socialists to pass significant policy measures that improved the lives of millions, like universal health care, vacation for all, and expansive labor rights. The growing power of the working class outside of the state at the time also helped conceal the problems that the social democrats’ increasingly electorally focused strategy would eventually face. As time wore on, however, social democrats in government found themselves constrained to merely managing capitalist economies — whose center of power lay not in the state but in the hands of private capital owners who could withhold or offshore their investments if they felt sufficiently threatened, causing economic turbulence and eventually leading to socialist electoral defeat. Many social democratic parties began abandoning the end goal of bringing about socialism entirely, focusing on achieving reforms within capitalism instead. The problem was worsened by the fact that the labor movement, social democrats’ traditional base of power, slowly ossified and came to represent an ever smaller proportion of the working class. In periods of economic stagnation, as in the 1970s and ’80s, this dynamic led socialist governments such as François Mitterrand’s in France to impose austerity measures in an attempt to appease capital and maintain growth. But this too ultimately undermined their popularity and brought about their electoral ousting. In recent decades, declining union density has accelerated this dynamic, leading desperate left-wing parties to try to cobble together broader populist coalitions in order to win a plurality of votes. But these parties have then found that they lacked the organized power outside of the state to overcome the leverage of capital once they entered government, as we saw with the collapse of Podemos in Spain and Syriza in Greece. The core reason that postwar social democratic parties failed, then, was not that party leaders betrayed their base, but that the structural economic conditions imposed by capitalist social relations give owners of capital significant power over the state, limiting socialists’ ability to implement policy reforms absent independent bases of popular power. Social democrats often took this structural imbalance of power between capital and workers outside of the state as an unchangeable given, adopting an electoralist approach at the expense of reconstituting working-class organization. An Alternative to Electoralism: a Democratic Socialist Electoral Strategy Observing the crisis of social democracy in the 1970s, the Marxist philosopher Nicos Poulantzas theorized a democratic socialist electoral strategy as an alternative to both Leninist insurrectionism and social democratic electoralism. For Poulantzas, the state was a terrain of struggle that could be used by socialists to enact transformative change, but only if it was used to help build independent working-class power that would solidify this change and shift power from capital to workers. Adam Przeworski developed this idea further with the concept of class formation. Przeworski argued that whether proletarians act on their class interests rather than their many other interests (as, e.g., homeowners or college graduates or Catholics) depends on whether a political struggle brings class interests to the fore. This struggle is not just about changing people’s ideas but also about changing the world to materially align people around their shared class interests. For example, socialists in Sweden significantly reduced the wage gap between different types of workers through their “ solidaristic wage policy,” thereby not only raising the floor for the lowest-paid workers and reshaping the economy around more efficient industries but also leveling material differences between different segments of the working class. Today the biggest challenge American socialists face is a politically fragmented working class and a weak labor movement decimated by decades of neoliberal attacks. A democratic socialist electoral strategy aims to use electoral campaigns and socialist governance to slowly rebuild working-class consciousness and organization in order to reconstitute the popular power needed to transform society. Such a strategy situates those efforts within a broader approach alongside equally necessary grassroots organizing in workplaces and neighborhoods. Using Elections to Agitate and Organize What does such an electoral strategy, as opposed to mere “electoralism,” look like in practice? For one thing, socialists can use campaign communications to clarify the lines of class struggle. Bernie Sanders’s presidential campaigns exemplified this approach to messaging, with his “Not Me, Us” language, his calls for political revolution, and his frequent finger-pointing at the billionaires who benefit from our current class society. Once in office, socialists can continue to raise people’s political awareness by pointing out when capital stands in the way of much-needed reform or is otherwise harming the interests of working people. Mayor Mamdani’s “Rental Ripoff Hearings” are an excellent example of this type of us-versus-them line drawing, as are Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s frequent viral denunciations of corporate greed in her House speeches. Electoral campaigns can also be used to build socialist organization, as DSA has done in recent years by building out volunteer-led organizing efforts that engage thousands of volunteers in outreach to the broader working class — not only reaching more voters but also developing activists who may continue organizing in the socialist movement for years to come. Socialists in office can go beyond changing peoples’ ideas too: they can use their political power to make it easier for workers, renters, and consumers to build collective organization, thereby increasing the potential power of the socialist movement in the long run. One way to facilitate working-class organization is to use the power of the state to bolster organizing directly, for example by helping tenants and workers organize through public offices dedicated to the task, as the Mamdani administration has begun to do with its Office of Tenant Protection and Office of Worker Power. When socialists have greater political power, they can also pass legislation that directly empowers organizing, like reforming labor law to make it easier to unionize or establishing enforceable collective bargaining rights for tenant unions. With enough power, socialists can start to change the broader structures of the economy to shift power from capital to the working class — for instance, by nationalizing key industries. Even smaller reforms along the way, such as rent freezes and reducing transit costs, can grow support for the socialist project while redistributing resources. Finally, a democratic socialist electoral strategy recognizes the limited power of elections alone on the road to socialism. While winning elections and passing legislation are an essential part of building political power, democratic socialists must equally prioritize building people power beyond elections through union, tenant, and social movement organizing. Recognizing what elections can’t do is as important as understanding how we can best use them to build power. Most socialists in the United States today believe in the importance of contesting elections and taking state power to make change. But as the movement grows, socialists should avoid the pitfalls of a pure-and-simple electoralism that focuses on electing candidates and getting policy passed to the exclusion of all else. Such an approach sets the movement up for disaster when capital brings its leverage to bear in the context of a disorganized working class. We should instead be pursuing a democratic socialist electoral strategy, using campaigns and elected office alongside grassroots organizing to help rebuild the independent bases of working-class power that will be needed to achieve socialism in the long run. articles.title: Battle Over Palestine's History
articles.author: Ramzy Baroud
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Three years into the Gaza genocide, Israel has exposed what its advocates spent more than a century trying to conceal: the violence underlying its claims of victimhood. The story of that concealment stretches back to the beginnings of organized political Zionism. The First Zionist Congress was held in Basel, Switzerland, on August 29–31, 1897. In the decades that followed, the Zionist movement, and eventually Israel, largely managed to hoodwink the world about Palestine and its people. From the slogan “a land without a people for a people without a land,” popularized in a similar form by Israel Zangwill, to Golda Meir’s declaration that “There was no such thing as Palestinians,” to Benjamin Netanyahu’s insistence that Israel has no Palestinian partner for peace, the language changed, but its purpose remained: to deny Palestinian existence, rights, or agency. Related: The Iran War, Israel Aid, and the Political Fallout for Trump Zionist advocates excelled in this realm of deception. Their discourse consisted of lies stacked one on top of another, creating a fantasy reinforced by Hollywood and mainstream media, until it came to substitute for the reality of Palestine. In this narrative, the victim became the aggressor, the refugee became the terrorist, and the colonizer became the hapless victim fighting for survival. The success of this inversion was not the outcome of the intellectual superiority of Zionist and Israeli advocates—a misconception even embraced by some Palestinians and Arabs. It was the outcome of coordinated efforts to present Zionist lies as truth while obfuscating, demonizing, and erasing the Palestinian narrative and silencing those who narrate it. That silencing has never been confined to words. Israel has historically killed those who challenge its account of Palestine. During the Gaza genocide, its direct assassinations of journalists, alongside its killing of intellectuals, historians, teachers, bloggers, and social media influencers, were meant to eliminate the storyteller; in Israel’s eyes, eliminating the storyteller means eliminating the story itself. Israel, however, miscalculated. Collective narratives of liberation, resistance, and the quest for justice are not an elitist enterprise dependent on an individual, or two, or even a thousand. They belong to a people. Killing those who tell the story cannot extinguish the collective experience from which it emerges. The more Israel killed, the more deeply the Palestinian narrative penetrated global consciousness. Israel’s own conduct compounded this failure. In the past, Israel would launch well-funded public relations campaigns to repair its image after footage of its wars against Palestinians or the Lebanese reached global audiences. This time, the power of the Palestinian narrative, particularly that emerging from Gaza itself, and the extent of Israel’s crimes in the Strip have made whitewashing genocide nearly impossible. Israel will try, however, backed by still-unapologetic mainstream media institutions and allies within Western societies who continue to justify its crimes. But the lines are now drawn more clearly: you are either against the genocide or with it. Denial offers no escape from that choice; it requires dismissing the evidence before the world’s eyes. This makes our task clearer as well. Related: Palestinians Beat Israel's Political System at Its Own Game In the past, we fought against more than a century of a carefully constructed Zionist narrative that largely went unchallenged in dominant Western institutions. Today, although the institutional balance remains unequal, Israel’s monopoly over the narrative has been broken. Israel still has its mainstream allies and apologists across ideological camps. Palestinians, however, have reached a global public increasingly critical of Israel. Pew Research Center’s spring 2026 survey found that, across 36 countries, a median of 67 percent of adults held an unfavorable view of Israel. This reveals how far Israel’s standing has deteriorated—and the opportunity Palestinians now have to turn greater awareness into sustained solidarity and accountability. The truth has always been on the Palestinian side. What has changed is our ability to communicate it to a global audience increasingly willing to listen. What needs to change now is how we build on that achievement. First, Palestinians must ensure that their righteous cause is not manipulated, abused, or used as political capital by any politician, party, or individual with a self-serving agenda. Greater visibility must not come at the expense of Palestinian ownership of their own struggle. Related: Netanyahu or Not, Israel's Occupation of Palestine Will Continue Second, they must avoid apologizing for their cause in the name of political compromise. Such apologies concede ground without securing rights. They also risk splintering our movement, turning political differences into divisions over the legitimacy of the struggle itself. Third, Palestinians must not confuse the pursuit of political solutions—which mean nothing to an enemy that continues to commit genocide—with the central task of exposing Israel, holding its war criminals accountable, and confronting the ideology underlying its crimes. Fourth, they must recognize that no future of peace, justice, or accountability can be achieved in the shadow of Zionism. This last point connects the present genocide to the longer history from which it emerged. Even when Netanyahu is long gone, and government power moves from one political camp to another, Zionism will remain. Indeed, the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians did not begin with Netanyahu, nor does its ideological foundation depend on his political survival. Zionism is the overriding principle, and Israel is the state that puts these plans into practice. Related: Empty Stadiums, No Accountability: Israel and the Sports Boycott Exposing Zionism will also help further globalize the Palestinian struggle, as this ideology wreaks havoc beyond Palestine, from the wider Middle East to Washington. Like imperialism, fascism, and Nazism, it must be confronted as an enemy of humanity. We want to believe that Israel will never be able to turn back the clock and again play the role of the victim, the face of civilization, or the so-called “villa in the jungle.” But the institutions that sustained those claims are still working to restore them. Exposing Israel’s crimes is only the beginning. Defeating apartheid, racism, and genocide requires sustained, selfless work to uproot the Zionist ideology that drives them. Greater global awareness must translate into action that secures Palestinian rights and freedom. We owe it to Gaza, to Palestine, and to humanity not to abandon this fight. Thinking Palestine

articles.title: The 1973 Athens Polytechnic Uprising Still Matters Today
articles.author: Christos Avramidis
articles.content: A military dictatorship had ruled Greece for more than six years when, in November 1973, hundreds of student occupied the Athens Polytechnic, transforming their university into a center of resistance. Thousands of workers, school students, and ordinary citizens soon joined them. On the pillars of the Polytechnic’s central gate, a student painted two messages in large letters: “USA OUT” and “NATO OUT.” Within days, on November 17, a military tank would smash through that same gate. Why were young Greeks risking their lives to overthrow the military dictatorship also demanding the withdrawal of the United States and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO)? The answer lies in the three decades preceding the uprising. During those years, Greece experienced Nazi occupation, British military intervention, civil war, and the consolidation of an anti-communist political order that American assistance sustained. The Greek ruling class was all too happy to allow US interference to consolidate its own rule. The Resistance That Britain Opposed During World War II, Greece developed one of Europe’s largest resistance movements. The communist-led National Liberation Front (EAM) and its armed wing, the Greek People’s Liberation Army (ELAS), mobilized hundreds of thousands of people and came to control much of the Greek countryside. EAM was far more than a guerrilla organization. In the territories it liberated from Nazi occupation, EAM established institutions of popular administration, organized schools, and introduced new forms of political participation. In 1944, women were able to vote and stand as candidates in elections the resistance organized, years before they gained equal voting rights in national Greek elections. By the time German troops withdrew in October 1944, the resistance had become one of the most powerful social and political forces in the country. But Winston Churchill’s government was determined to prevent the communist-led movement from dominating postwar Greece. The confrontation centered on the future of the armed forces. Under British supervision, the Greek government demanded the disarmament of ELAS while retaining military formations associated with the government in exile. EAM rejected an arrangement that would leave its supporters disarmed in the face of potentially hostile forces. In practice, the leadership of EAM and of the Communist Party of Greece had an ambivalent stance toward the British army and British agents operating on Greek soil. They had cooperated with the British against the Nazi occupation. But they were deeply skeptical of British intervention in liberated Greece. Events after the German withdrawal from Athens confirmed their suspicions: the forces of liberation (EAM/ELAS and their allies) would have to fight a new battle. On December 3, 1944, an enormous, initially peaceful demonstration gathered in central Athens. Police opened fire, killing demonstrators and wounding many others. The Athens police chief, Angelos Evert, later acknowledged ordering the shooting. He had remained in charge of the police during the Nazi occupation, maintaining relations with the occupying authorities as well as contacts with British intelligence. The massacre marked the beginning of the December clashes, which Greeks call the Dekemvriana . British troops clashed with ELAS in the streets of Athens, using tanks, artillery, and aircraft. Their Greek allies included formations containing former members of the Security Battalions, which had collaborated with the Nazi occupiers in the struggle against the resistance. Militants who had fought the Nazis now faced the British army — and, fighting alongside it, former collaborators of the occupation. Churchill himself arrived in Athens on Christmas Day to intervene in the political negotiations. The British military campaign eventually defeated ELAS in the capital. The Varkiza Agreement, which the government and EAM signed in February 1945, then required the resistance to surrender its weapons. The Left had suffered a military defeat and now had to accept a political settlement from a position of profound weakness. Its supporters would soon discover how little protection that settlement provided. White Terror and the American Takeover Widespread persecution of the Left, which Greeks remember as the White Terror, followed the disarmament of ELAS. Armed right-wing groups, often operating with the tolerance or cooperation of state authorities, targeted people associated with EAM. They murdered and tortured former resistance fighters or drove them from their homes. State authorities imprisoned many more. Contemporary figures that EAM compiled recorded 1,289 murders, 31,632 cases of torture and physical abuse, 84,931 arrests, and 265 rapes between February 1945 and March 1946. United Nations documentation later cited these figures, but they originated with the persecuted movement rather than an independent nationwide investigation. The political climate was hardly conducive to a free electoral contest. The government scheduled elections for March 1946, while thousands of leftists faced imprisonment, displacement, intimidation, and restrictions on political activity. The communist-led left boycotted the vote, arguing that the conditions made meaningful democratic participation impossible. The Right emerged victorious. A referendum later that year restored King George II to the throne, consolidating the monarchy’s influence in the postwar political order. Greece descended into full-scale civil war. By 1947, however, Britain could no longer afford to sustain its intervention. The United States took its place. President Harry Truman requested $400 million in assistance for Greece and Turkey, declaring that Washington would help free peoples resist communist domination. In Greece, this meant massive military assistance to the government fighting the communist-led Democratic Army of Greece (DSE). American weapons, money, and military advisers helped determine the outcome of the war. During its final stages in 1949, Greek government aircraft dropped American-supplied napalm on Greek territory, targeting communist positions in the mountains of northern Greece. The United States had used napalm during World War II, but its deployment in Greece preceded Washington’s much better-known use of the weapon in Vietnam. Government forces defeated the DSE in 1949. For their supporters, however, the end of the war did not bring freedom. The iconic image of Greek resistance fighter Nikos Beloyannis holding a red carnation. ( Femmes françaises / Gallica Digital Library) The state sent thousands of leftists to prisons and remote island camps. The camp on the island of Makronisos became particularly notorious for its system of torture, beatings, forced declarations of repentance, and ideological reeducation. The contrast with the treatment of Nazi collaborators was striking, with far higher numbers of executions. One execution became a symbol of that political order. Nikos Beloyannis had been a communist resistance fighter during the Nazi occupation. The authorities arrested him after the civil war, and a military court sentenced him to death. A photograph of him smiling with a red carnation during his trial became famous internationally, while an international campaign demanded that the Greek government spare his life. Nevertheless, on March 30, 1952, a firing squad executed Beloyannis and three other communists. Their deaths reflected the determination of the postwar Greek state to eliminate what it regarded as the communist threat, despite the formal restoration of parliamentary institutions. That same year, Greece joined NATO. Much of Greece’s political elite had fled the country during the Nazi occupation, while significant sections of its economic elite had collaborated with the occupying forces. After liberation, the former returned to power, while much of the latter retained its economic influence. The restored ruling establishment built new mechanisms of repression and presided over a new era for Greek capitalism, keeping wages low and suppressing trade unions. US imperialism, which had taken the reins from its British counterpart, underpinned this new configuration of forces. In the postwar years, US interference would take many forms; at the same time, the Greek left would prove much more resilient than anyone could have predicted. When the American Ambassador Intervened in Greek Elections American influence went beyond supplying weapons. Declassified US diplomatic documents reveal direct American intervention in Greece’s electoral arrangements. In March 1952, US ambassador John Peurifoy informed Washington that the American embassy’s political intervention and a public statement had blocked the introduction of proportional representation. The American ambassador was candidly discussing his government’s efforts to influence the electoral system of a formally sovereign democracy. The elections four years later vividly illustrated the political consequences of Greece’s unusual electoral arrangements. In the 1956 parliamentary elections, the opposition Democratic Union won 48.15 percent of the popular vote, compared with 47.38 percent for Konstantinos Karamanlis’s conservative National Radical Union. Yet Karamanlis secured 165 parliamentary seats, while the opposition received only 132. The party that won fewer votes formed the new government. The opposition alliance was not a communist electoral front. It brought together centrist and left-wing forces against the conservative government. Even this broad parliamentary challenge failed to dislodge the Right. Two years later, the United Democratic Left (EDA) became Greece’s second-largest parliamentary party, demonstrating the continuing electoral strength of the Left despite years of persecution. The result alarmed the conservative establishment and reinforced its fears about the political consequences of a more open democratic system. The Monarchy, the Para-State, and the Road to Dictatorship The Greek monarchy was far from a ceremonial institution. The palace intervened repeatedly in political affairs, exercised substantial influence over the armed forces, and helped shape the composition and survival of governments. Alongside the formal state existed an extensive anti-communist security apparatus and networks of right-wing organizations, some of which maintained close relations with elements of the police, military, and intelligence services. Greek and American security agencies also cooperated during the Cold War in covert structures, including a clandestine stay-behind network called “Red Sheepskin.” These networks formed part of the country’s anti-communist security architecture, although their existence alone does not establish responsibility for every episode of political violence. In 1965, King Constantine II’s confrontation with the centrist Prime Minister Georgios Papandreou over control of the military precipitated a government crisis. Papandreou had won a substantial parliamentary majority in 1964, yet his government collapsed amid royal intervention and defections from his own party. Greeks call these defections the Apostasia . The conflict was particularly revealing because Papandreou was no communist revolutionary. He was a moderate centrist politician operating within the parliamentary system. Nevertheless, his attempt to exercise authority over the military collided with the monarchy and the security establishment. By April 1967, Greece was approaching another national election. The army intervened before voters could go to the polls. The Colonels and Their American Allies On April 21, 1967, a group of military officers seized power. They suspended the constitution, banned political parties, imposed censorship, and arrested thousands of political opponents. The dictatorship established a system of exile and torture that particularly targeted communists, trade unionists, students, and other opponents. Its leaders justified their seizure of power as necessary to prevent a communist takeover. The precise extent of American foreknowledge of the coup, and of individual US officials’ involvement in it, remains contested. But the documentary record of Washington’s subsequent military cooperation with the dictatorship is extensive and undisputed. The Johnson administration suspended deliveries of certain major weapons systems. The suspension, however, was only partial, and restrictions on military deliveries were gradually eased. An October 1969 memorandum for President Richard Nixon acknowledged that the United States had delivered approximately $100 million in military equipment to Greece as grant assistance between April 1967 and June 1969. During the same period, the dictatorship held political prisoners in camps and prisons, and torture and repression continued unabated. American officials had a clear understanding of the nature of the dictatorship. They also regarded Greece’s position in NATO, its military installations, and its strategic location in the eastern Mediterranean as important to American interests. The contradiction was evident. Washington publicly called for constitutional government while maintaining significant military ties with a dictatorship that had abolished it. Greece was not an isolated example. In Spain, the United States had signed military agreements with Francisco Franco’s dictatorship in 1953, securing access to bases in exchange for financial and military assistance. The protection of Western strategic interests could coexist with the survival of authoritarian governments. The Tank at the Athens Polytechnic Uprising By November 1973, the Greek dictatorship was facing growing opposition. On November 14, students occupied the Athens Polytechnic and established a makeshift radio station. Their broadcasts called on the population to join the struggle for freedom. The most famous slogan of the uprising was “Bread, Education, Freedom.” But the messages painted on the pillars of the university gate revealed another dimension of the revolt. They read “USA OUT” and “NATO OUT.” For the protesters, these demands were inseparable from their struggle against the dictatorship. They had grown up in a country where American military assistance had helped defeat the communist left and where political prisoners had endured years of persecution. US diplomats had intervened in its domestic politics, and Greece’s military dictatorship maintained close relations with Washington. Thousands gathered around the Polytechnic. In the early hours of November 17, the dictatorship sent tanks against the occupied university. One crashed through the main gate. Police and soldiers violently suppressed the uprising. Historian Leonidas Kallivretakis has documented twenty-four confirmed deaths associated with the events, many of them in the streets surrounding the Polytechnic. In Greek popular memory, the uprising became the decisive event that brought down the dictatorship. Strictly speaking, however, the dictatorship survived for another eight months. On November 25, hard-line military officer Dimitrios Ioannidis overthrew dictator Georgios Papadopoulos and established an even more repressive military government. But Greek society had watched police and soldiers kill young people who had demanded freedom. The apparent restoration of military control could not erase the political consequences of the uprising. American officials continued to maintain diplomatic and military relations with the new junta, despite their awareness of its repressive character. US diplomatic reporting from 1974 acknowledged the resentment directed at Washington and the widespread Greek belief that American support had contributed to the dictatorship’s survival. The new rulers also maintained their interest in relations with the United States while seeking international support for their rule. The junta finally collapsed in July 1974, after it organized a coup against Cyprus’s president, Archbishop Makarios III, triggering the crisis that culminated in Turkey’s invasion of the island. Democracy returned. But the legacy of the Polytechnic uprising extended far beyond the overthrow of the colonels. The Bases That Never Left The anger against foreign intervention remained a powerful force in Greek politics after the restoration of democracy. In August 1974, even conservative Prime Minister Karamanlis withdrew Greece from NATO’s integrated military command structure in protest over the alliance’s response to Turkey’s invasion of Cyprus. The decision reflected both the government’s security concerns and the extraordinary public anger surrounding the Cyprus crisis. Greece returned to NATO’s military command in 1980. In October 1981, Andreas Papandreou, the son of Georgios Papandreou, led the Panhellenic Socialist Movement (PASOK) to victory. PASOK won 48.07 percent of the vote, the highest share in the party’s electoral history. Its program had promised a fundamental change in Greece’s relationship with the United States, including the removal of American bases and withdrawal from NATO, but neither happened. In 1983, Papandreou’s government signed a new agreement regulating the American military presence. The country remained in NATO, and American facilities continued operating. More than fifty years later, Greece remains an important part of American military strategy. Successive governments have expanded defense cooperation with Washington, including agreements granting American forces access to facilities across the country. Among the most significant is Souda Bay, on the island of Crete, a major logistical and operational hub for the US Navy and Air Force in the eastern Mediterranean. The implications became particularly visible during the American attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. Greek news outlets reported that American KC-135 aerial refueling aircraft operating from Souda Bay supported the mission involving US B-2 bombers. According to these reports, aircraft departing from the base participated in refueling operations over the Mediterranean. In March 2026, the United States, Israel, and Iran were once again locked in military confrontation. Greece’s defense minister, Nikos Dendias, publicly discussed the possibility of attacks on military facilities and the measures the government had taken to protect Souda Bay and other critical infrastructure. The Greek government has stated that Greece is not participating in operations against Iran. But the strategic importance of American military facilities on Greek territory has made questions about their use, security, and accountability increasingly consequential. The Polytechnic Uprising Lives On Every November 17, tens of thousands of Greeks take to the streets to commemorate the Polytechnic uprising. The annual march traditionally ends outside the American embassy. Even the statue of Harry S. Truman in Athens became a target of protest. Over the decades, demonstrators repeatedly attacked it and attempted to bring it down, sometimes succeeding. The monument to the president whose doctrine had initiated America’s postwar intervention in Greece became a recurring symbol of opposition to that intervention. The dictatorship fell in 1974. Parliamentary democracy returned, and governments of different political orientations have held power since then. Yet the country continues to host military facilities that form part of Washington’s wider strategic presence in the Mediterranean and the Middle East. For generations of Greeks, the Polytechnic has represented not only the struggle against military dictatorship but also the demand that the country’s future should be decided by its own people. Fifty-three years after the uprising, the words students painted on the pillars of its gate remain part of an unresolved historical debate. A tank smashed the gate. The demands written on its pillars survived. articles.title: Local 256 Secures New Contract, Maintains Union Shop
articles.content: Local 256 (MIT-GSU) ratified a new three-year contract with MIT on November 16. They successfully negotiated raises that keep up with inflation — the members will receive a wage increase of 3.5 percent in 2026 (with retroactive pay), 3.25 percent in 2027, and 3.25 percent in 2028. The members gained vacation flexibility, kept their healthcare benefits, and negotiated increased protections for international workers. The local also retained their union shop by organizing an effective strike threat that forced MIT to back down from their demand for an open shop. Local 256 Vice President of Membership Suveena Sreenilayam said, “We are incredibly excited to have won a fair second contract when it was the last thing MIT wanted to do. We know that building a credible strike threat is the only reason MIT was motivated to settle on all of our strike issues. “MIT came into these contract negotiations trying to gut our union by proposing an open shop. On Tuesday, we not only won back our union shop, we organized for protections that meet the moment, like an immigration support fund for international workers. This is thanks to every member and the tens of thousands of conversations we had over the past year to build our union power.” Stay tuned for more details about the contract and the organizational campaign that won it in the coming weeks.
